tracks.publicName: Where to go about a Nebraska pardon
tracks.mechanism: The Nebraska Board of Pardons, composed of the Governor, the Attorney General and the Secretary of State, grants pardons. A pardon nullifies the conviction, is the only route to firearm-rights restoration, and is the prerequisite to sealing a pardoned conviction. The judiciary publishes the Board's waiting periods as ten years for felonies and three years for misdemeanors, restarting on any contact with law enforcement or additional conviction, and records that the Board will not consider pardons for traffic violations, driving under the influence, or driving under suspension.
exclusions: Traffic violations, driving under the influence and driving under suspension, which the Board will not consider.

tracks.venue: No court venue. The Board of Pardons is an executive body.

tracks.legalName: Automatic Annulment of a Non-Conviction Disposed of On or After January 1, 2019 (RSA 651:5, II-a(a))
tracks.publicName: Your dismissed or not-guilty New Hampshire case should clear itself
tracks.mechanism: New Hampshire calls this annulment, not expungement or sealing. Where a person is found not guilty on all charges that resulted from the arrest, or the case is dismissed or not prosecuted, and the offence was disposed of on or after January 1, 2019, the arrest record and court record shall be annulled thirty days after the finding if no appeal is taken under RSA 606:10, or on final determination of an appeal affirming the dismissal. There is no petition, no fee, no hearing and nothing to file. Under RSA 651:5, X(a) the person is treated in all respects as if never arrested, convicted or sentenced. Court records are sealed with the limited access list at X(c). The arresting and prosecuting agencies must clearly identify the annulment in their files and electronic records. Law enforcement retains records under XI(b) and may share them for legitimate investigative purposes, in defense of a civil suit arising from the arrest, and with the police standards and training council. A prior conviction may still be considered at sentencing on a later crime and may count toward habitual offender status under RSA 259:39. Under XVI and XVII no journalist, person or entity faces any penalty for publishing an annulled record or for not removing or correcting an earlier report, which is the statutory reason private background-check databases keep showing the case.
exclusions: Offences disposed of before January 1, 2019, which need a petition under RSA 651:5, II.
A not-guilty finding on only some of the charges resulting from the arrest. The automatic route needs all of them.
Federal, military, tribal and out-of-state records. A New Hampshire annulment does not reach them and the federal government does not recognise it.

A prior conviction may still be considered at sentencing on a later crime and may count toward habitual offender status under RSA 259:39. Under XVI and XVII no journalist, person or entity faces any penalty for publishing an annulled record or for not removing or correcting an earlier report, which is the statutory reason private background-check databases keep showing the case.
exclusions: Offences outside paragraph II-a, which need a petition under RSA 651:5, II.

tracks.legalName: Petition to Annul the Record of a Non-Conviction Disposed of Before January 1, 2019 (RSA 651:5, II)
tracks.publicName: Annul an older New Hampshire arrest that did not end in a conviction
tracks.mechanism: A person found not guilty, or whose case was dismissed or not prosecuted, may petition at any time for annulment of the arrest record, the court record, or both, where the offence was disposed of before January 1, 2019 or otherwise falls outside the automatic route in paragraph II-a. Relief is discretionary under paragraph I: the court may annul if in its opinion the annulment will assist rehabilitation and be consistent with the public welfare, and it may grant or deny without a hearing unless the petitioner requests one. The court provides a copy of the petition to the prosecutor, who may be heard on the interest of justice, and the Department of Corrections performs a statutory investigation. RSA 651:5, IX and X(d) exempt a person found not guilty or whose case was dismissed or not prosecuted from the $100 Department of Corrections investigation fee and the $100 Department of Safety and state police fees. Under RSA 651:5, X(a) the person is treated in all respects as if never arrested, convicted or sentenced. Court records are sealed with the limited access list at X(c). The arresting and prosecuting agencies must clearly identify the annulment in their files and electronic records. Law enforcement retains records under XI(b) and may share them for legitimate investigative purposes, in defense of a civil suit arising from the arrest, and with the police standards and training council. A prior conviction may still be considered at sentencing on a later crime and may count toward habitual offender status under RSA 259:39. Under XVI and XVII no journalist, person or entity faces any penalty for publishing an annulled record or for not removing or correcting an earlier report, which is the statutory reason private background-check databases keep showing the case.
exclusions: Offences disposed of on or after January 1, 2019, which are annulled automatically under RSA 651:5, II-a(a) with no petition and no fee.
Federal, military, tribal and out-of-state records.
A further petition within 3 years of a denial, barred by RSA 651:5, IV.

tracks.legalName: Petition to Annul the Record of a Vacated Conviction Outside the Automatic Route (RSA 651:5, II, second sentence)
tracks.publicName: Annul the record of a New Hampshire conviction that was vacated
tracks.mechanism: A person convicted of a criminal offence whose conviction was subsequently vacated by a court may petition for annulment where the offence falls outside the automatic route in paragraph II-a. There is no waiting period. Relief is discretionary under paragraph I and the court may decide without a hearing unless the petitioner requests one. The procedure, the form family, the investigation, the prosecutor's opportunity to be heard and the effect are the same as on the pre-2019 non-conviction petition; the difference is cost, because the RSA 651:5, IX and X(d) fee exemptions are written around not-guilty, dismissed and not-prosecuted cases and on the face of the statute do not reach a vacated conviction. Under RSA 651:5, X(a) the person is treated in all respects as if never arrested, convicted or sentenced. Court records are sealed with the limited access list at X(c). The arresting and prosecuting agencies must clearly identify the annulment in their files and electronic records. Law enforcement retains records under XI(b) and may share them for legitimate investigative purposes, in defense of a civil suit arising from the arrest, and with the police standards and training council. A prior conviction may still be considered at sentencing on a later crime and may count toward habitual offender status under RSA 259:39. Under XVI and XVII no journalist, person or entity faces any penalty for publishing an annulled record or for not removing or correcting an earlier report, which is the statutory reason private background-check databases keep showing the case.
exclusions: Vacated convictions inside paragraph II-a, which are annulled automatically with no petition and no fee.
An order that is a reversal, a set-aside, a new trial order or a sentence modification rather than a vacatur.
Federal, military, tribal and out-of-state records.
A further petition within 3 years of a denial, barred by RSA 651:5, IV.

rules.serviceCertificateOnNhjb2328: NHJB-2328-DFPe* (01/01/2018) is the financial statement that accompanies the NHJB-2311-Se (07/01/2018) motion for waiver of filing fee: the motion is the waiver request, the statement supports it. The statement's third page carries its own service certification, verbatim: "I state that on this date I am sending a copy of this document as required by the rules of the Circuit Court. I am electronically sending this document through the court's electronic filing system to all attorneys and to all other parties who have entered electronic service contacts (email addresses) in this case. I am mailing or hand-delivering copies to all other interested parties." That is service text, not evidence that service has occurred: the certificate's checkbox, signature and date stay blank in the packet until service actually occurs, the packet never says the held statement has no service instruction, and no e-service representation is transplanted into a paper filing or another court workflow without confirmation. The petition's own service answer stands (none by the participant; the court transmits the petition to the prosecutor under RSA 651:5, IX), and RSA 651:5, IX does not expressly settle service of the separate financial statement. Recorded 2026-09-06 from the research handoff.

tracks.legalName: Petition to Annul the Record of Arrest, Conviction and Sentence, Standard Route (RSA 651:5, III(a)(1), (b)(1) and (c) through (i))
tracks.publicName: Annul your New Hampshire conviction
tracks.mechanism: New Hampshire calls this annulment of the record of arrest, conviction and sentence. A petition may be brought after the waiting period for the offence class has run from completion of all terms and conditions of the sentence, with no other conviction in that period except a motor vehicle violation other than DWI. Relief is discretionary: paragraph I lets the court annul if the annulment will assist rehabilitation and be consistent with the public welfare, and the court may decide without a hearing unless the petitioner requests one. Three rules make eligibility a whole-record question rather than a per-case one. Paragraph V bars any violent crime, any felony obstruction crime and any extended-term sentence outright. Paragraph VI forbids annulment where any part of the record is barred, or until the time requirements for all offenses of record have been met. Paragraph VIII dismisses a non-qualifying petition without a hearing, and paragraph IV then bars a further petition for three years. Under RSA 651:5, X(a) the person is treated in all respects as if never arrested, convicted or sentenced. Court records are sealed with the limited access list at X(c). The arresting and prosecuting agencies must clearly identify the annulment in their files and electronic records. Law enforcement retains records under XI(b) and may share them for legitimate investigative purposes, in defense of a civil suit arising from the arrest, and with the police standards and training council. A prior conviction may still be considered at sentencing on a later crime and may count toward habitual offender status under RSA 259:39. Under XVI and XVII no journalist, person or entity faces any penalty for publishing an annulled record or for not removing or correcting an earlier report, which is the statutory reason private background-check databases keep showing the case.
exclusions: Any violent crime as defined by RSA 651:5, XIII: capital, first or second degree murder, manslaughter or class A felony negligent homicide under RSA 630; first degree assault under RSA 631:1; aggravated felonious sexual assault or felonious sexual assault under RSA 632-A; kidnapping or criminal restraint under RSA 633; class A felony arson under RSA 634:1; robbery under RSA 636; incest under RSA 639:2, III or endangering the welfare of a child by solicitation under RSA 639:3, III; and any felonious offense involving child sexual abuse images under RSA 649-A. RSA 651:5, V.

Any crime of obstruction of justice as defined by RSA 651:5, XIV: tampering with witnesses or informants under RSA 641:5, falsifying evidence under RSA 641:6, or any felonious offense of obstructing governmental operations under RSA 642. RSA 651:5, V.
Any offense for which the petitioner was sentenced to an extended term of imprisonment under RSA 651:6. RSA 651:5, V.

Any record where annulment of any part is barred under RSA 651:5, V, or where the time requirements under paragraphs III and IV have not been met for all offenses of record. RSA 651:5, VI freezes the whole record on one ineligible entry.
Impaired-driving convictions within RSA 265-A:21, which RSA 651:5, III excepts and which run on their own ten-year clock.
A further petition within 3 years of a denial. RSA 651:5, IV.
Federal, military, tribal and out-of-state records.

generationRequirements.question: What is your full legal name?
What is your date of birth?
Where should the court write to you?
Which court disposed of the charge, and where is it?
What is the case number and, if you have it, the charge ID?
For the charge you want annulled: what was the offence called, which RSA was violated, and on what date did it happen?
Was the offence a violation, a class B misdemeanor, a class A misdemeanor, or a felony — and if a felony, what class?
generationRequirements.conditionDescription: Asked because each level carries a different waiting period under RSA 651:5, III and misclassification either wastes a filing or triggers a paragraph VIII dismissal and a three-year lockout. Answered from the court record, not recollection.

generationRequirements.question: On what date were you convicted?
generationRequirements.conditionDescription: Asked because the January 1, 2019 line selects the form and, for a violation or class B misdemeanor, may route to the streamlined mandatory route instead.

generationRequirements.question: What sentence was imposed?
On what date did you finish every term and condition of the sentence, including probation or parole, fines, fees and restitution?
generationRequirements.conditionDescription: Asked because the waiting period runs from the day after all terms and conditions are complete, and because sentence completion is one of only two grounds on which a prosecutor may object to a streamlined petition.

generationRequirements.question: List every other conviction you have anywhere, with what it was, where, when, and when you finished that sentence.
generationRequirements.conditionDescription: Asked because RSA 651:5, VI makes eligibility a whole-record question: no annulment may be granted until the time requirements for all offenses of record have been met, and none may be granted if any part of the record is barred.

generationRequirements.question: Do any of those convictions come from outside New Hampshire, and if so what was the conduct?
generationRequirements.conditionDescription: Asked because RSA 651:5, VI-a excludes an out-of-state conviction for conduct that would not be an offense under New Hampshire law, which can unfreeze a record that otherwise looks blocked.

generationRequirements.question: Have you been convicted of anything since you finished that sentence, apart from a motor vehicle violation?
generationRequirements.conditionDescription: Asked because RSA 651:5, III requires a clean period, excepting motor vehicle violations other than DWI under RSA 265-A:2, I, RSA 265:82 or RSA 265:82-a.

generationRequirements.question: Is any charge pending against you now, anywhere?
generationRequirements.conditionDescription: Asked because RSA 651:5, VII stops the court acting on the petition until the pending charge is disposed of.

generationRequirements.question: Were you sentenced to an extended term of imprisonment on any of these convictions?
generationRequirements.conditionDescription: Asked as a routing screen, because RSA 651:5, V bars annulment outright. A yes or an unclear answer stops the track.

generationRequirements.question: Have you asked a New Hampshire court to annul any record before, and was it denied? If so, when?
generationRequirements.conditionDescription: Asked because RSA 651:5, IV bars a further petition more frequently than every 3 years after a denial.

generationRequirements.question: Do you need to ask the court to waive the $125.00 filing fee, or to be excused from the $100 investigation fee?
generationRequirements.conditionDescription: Asked so NHJB-2311 and NHJB-2328 are included where they are needed. RSA 651:5, IX excuses the investigation fee on a demonstration of indigency.

generationRequirements.question: Do you want to ask the court for a hearing? The court can decide without one.
generationRequirements.conditionDescription: Asked because RSA 651:5, I lets the court grant or deny without a hearing unless the petitioner requests one.

tracks.legalName: Petition of Eligibility for Annulment of a Violation or Class B Misdemeanor Conviction, Streamlined Mandatory Route (RSA 651:5, III(a)(2) and III(b)(2))
tracks.publicName: The fast New Hampshire annulment route for a recent minor conviction
tracks.mechanism: For a violation or a class B misdemeanor with a conviction date on or after January 1, 2019 where that offence was the highest offense of conviction, the court submits a notice of its determination to the person and to the prosecutor. The prosecutor has twenty days from receipt to object, and only on two grounds: that the offence is not eligible for annulment, or that the person has not completed all the terms and conditions of the sentence. If no timely objection is made, or the objection is denied, the court shall annul the conviction. This is the only conviction route in New Hampshire where the paragraph I rehabilitation and public welfare discretion does not decide the outcome, and the only one with a defined objection clock and defined objection grounds. Paragraphs V, VI, VII and VIII still apply. Under RSA 651:5, X(a) the person is treated in all respects as if never arrested, convicted or sentenced. Court records are sealed with the limited access list at X(c). The arresting and prosecuting agencies must clearly identify the annulment in their files and electronic records. Law enforcement retains records under XI(b) and may share them for legitimate investigative purposes, in defense of a civil suit arising from the arrest, and with the police standards and training council. A prior conviction may still be considered at sentencing on a later crime and may count toward habitual offender status under RSA 259:39. Under XVI and XVII no journalist, person or entity faces any penalty for publishing an annulled record or for not removing or correcting an earlier report, which is the statutory reason private background-check databases keep showing the case.
exclusions: A violation that is an offense specified under RSA 259:39, or another violation carrying an enhanced penalty for a subsequent conviction. Carved out of the violation row.
Sexual assault under RSA 632-A:4 and misdemeanor domestic violence under RSA 631:2-b. Carved out of the class B misdemeanor row.
Any offence that was not the highest offense of conviction in its case, which routes to the standard conviction route instead.
Convictions dated before January 1, 2019.

Any violent crime as defined by RSA 651:5, XIII: capital, first or second degree murder, manslaughter or class A felony negligent homicide under RSA 630; first degree assault under RSA 631:1; aggravated felonious sexual assault or felonious sexual assault under RSA 632-A; kidnapping or criminal restraint under RSA 633; class A felony arson under RSA 634:1; robbery under RSA 636; incest under RSA 639:2, III or endangering the welfare of a child by solicitation under RSA 639:3, III; and any felonious offense involving child sexual abuse images under RSA 649-A. RSA 651:5, V.

Any crime of obstruction of justice as defined by RSA 651:5, XIV: tampering with witnesses or informants under RSA 641:5, falsifying evidence under RSA 641:6, or any felonious offense of obstructing governmental operations under RSA 642. RSA 651:5, V.
Any offense for which the petitioner was sentenced to an extended term of imprisonment under RSA 651:6. RSA 651:5, V.

Any record where annulment of any part is barred under RSA 651:5, V, or where the time requirements under paragraphs III and IV have not been met for all offenses of record. RSA 651:5, VI freezes the whole record on one ineligible entry.
Impaired-driving convictions within RSA 265-A:21, which RSA 651:5, III excepts and which run on their own ten-year clock.
A further petition within 3 years of a denial. RSA 651:5, IV.
Federal, military, tribal and out-of-state records.

generationRequirements.question: What is your full legal name?
What is your date of birth?
Where should the court write to you?
Which court disposed of the charge, and where is it?
What is the case number and, if you have it, the charge ID?
For the charge you want annulled: what was the offence called, which RSA was violated, and on what date did it happen?
Was the offence a violation, a class B misdemeanor, a class A misdemeanor, or a felony — and if a felony, what class?
generationRequirements.conditionDescription: Asked because each level carries a different waiting period under RSA 651:5, III and misclassification either wastes a filing or triggers a paragraph VIII dismissal and a three-year lockout. Answered from the court record, not recollection.

generationRequirements.question: On what date were you convicted?
generationRequirements.conditionDescription: Asked because the January 1, 2019 line selects the form and, for a violation or class B misdemeanor, may route to the streamlined mandatory route instead.

generationRequirements.question: What sentence was imposed?
On what date did you finish every term and condition of the sentence, including probation or parole, fines, fees and restitution?
generationRequirements.conditionDescription: Asked because the waiting period runs from the day after all terms and conditions are complete, and because sentence completion is one of only two grounds on which a prosecutor may object to a streamlined petition.

generationRequirements.question: List every other conviction you have anywhere, with what it was, where, when, and when you finished that sentence.
generationRequirements.conditionDescription: Asked because RSA 651:5, VI makes eligibility a whole-record question: no annulment may be granted until the time requirements for all offenses of record have been met, and none may be granted if any part of the record is barred.

generationRequirements.question: Do any of those convictions come from outside New Hampshire, and if so what was the conduct?
generationRequirements.conditionDescription: Asked because RSA 651:5, VI-a excludes an out-of-state conviction for conduct that would not be an offense under New Hampshire law, which can unfreeze a record that otherwise looks blocked.

generationRequirements.question: Have you been convicted of anything since you finished that sentence, apart from a motor vehicle violation?
generationRequirements.conditionDescription: Asked because RSA 651:5, III requires a clean period, excepting motor vehicle violations other than DWI under RSA 265-A:2, I, RSA 265:82 or RSA 265:82-a.

generationRequirements.question: Is any charge pending against you now, anywhere?
generationRequirements.conditionDescription: Asked because RSA 651:5, VII stops the court acting on the petition until the pending charge is disposed of.

generationRequirements.question: Were you sentenced to an extended term of imprisonment on any of these convictions?
generationRequirements.conditionDescription: Asked as a routing screen, because RSA 651:5, V bars annulment outright. A yes or an unclear answer stops the track.

generationRequirements.question: Have you asked a New Hampshire court to annul any record before, and was it denied? If so, when?
generationRequirements.conditionDescription: Asked because RSA 651:5, IV bars a further petition more frequently than every 3 years after a denial.

generationRequirements.question: Do you need to ask the court to waive the $125.00 filing fee, or to be excused from the $100 investigation fee?
generationRequirements.conditionDescription: Asked so NHJB-2311 and NHJB-2328 are included where they are needed. RSA 651:5, IX excuses the investigation fee on a demonstration of indigency.

generationRequirements.question: Do you want to ask the court for a hearing? The court can decide without one.
generationRequirements.conditionDescription: Asked because RSA 651:5, I lets the court grant or deny without a hearing unless the petitioner requests one.

generationRequirements.question: In that case, was this the most serious offence you were convicted of, or were there others at the same or a higher level?
generationRequirements.conditionDescription: Asked because "highest offense of conviction" is the gate for this route. It is not on the face of most participants' recollection and must be answered from the court record, so a yes routes here and anything else routes to the standard conviction route.

generationRequirements.question: For a violation: is it an offence that counts toward habitual offender status under RSA 259:39, or one that carries a heavier penalty for a second conviction?
generationRequirements.conditionDescription: Asked because both are carved out of the violation row of this route.

tracks.legalName: Petition of Eligibility for Annulment of the Record of Arrest or Conviction for Personal Possession of Marijuana (RSA 651:5-b)
tracks.publicName: Annul an old New Hampshire marijuana possession record
tracks.mechanism: A person arrested for or convicted of knowingly or purposely obtaining, purchasing, transporting or possessing, actually or constructively, or having under control, three quarters of an ounce of marijuana or less, where the offence occurred before September 16, 2017, may petition at any time for annulment of the arrest record, the court record, or both. The petition states that the amount was three quarters of an ounce or less. The petitioner, not the court, furnishes a copy to the office of the prosecutor of the underlying offence. The prosecutor may object within ten days of receipt and request a hearing; if no timely objection is made the court shall grant the petition, and if the prosecutor objects the court holds a hearing at which the prosecutor must prove beyond a reasonable doubt that the amount exceeded three quarters of an ounce, failing which the court shall grant the petition. If granted, RSA 651:5, X and XI apply in full. Under RSA 651:5, X(a) the person is treated in all respects as if never arrested, convicted or sentenced. Court records are sealed with the limited access list at X(c). The arresting and prosecuting agencies must clearly identify the annulment in their files and electronic records. Law enforcement retains records under XI(b) and may share them for legitimate investigative purposes, in defense of a civil suit arising from the arrest, and with the police standards and training council. A prior conviction may still be considered at sentencing on a later crime and may count toward habitual offender status under RSA 259:39. Under XVI and XVII no journalist, person or entity faces any penalty for publishing an annulled record or for not removing or correcting an earlier report, which is the statutory reason private background-check databases keep showing the case.
exclusions: Offences occurring on or after September 16, 2017, which are outside the section.
Any amount exceeding three quarters of an ounce.
Any offence involving sale, distribution or intent to distribute rather than the personal-possession verbs the section lists.
Federal, military, tribal and out-of-state records.

tracks.legalName: Annulment of a New Hampshire Supreme Court Record (RSA 651:5, XV)
tracks.publicName: Records of a New Hampshire appeal
tracks.mechanism: A petition for annulment authorized by RSA 651:5 may be brought in the supreme court with respect to any such record in the supreme court, except that no supreme court record relating to an opinion published in the New Hampshire Reports may be annulled. No form is published for it and appellate practice is not self-help territory, so LegalEase detects the situation where a participant's case went up on appeal, names the section, discloses that a published opinion can never be annulled, and refers.
exclusions: Any supreme court record relating to an opinion published in the New Hampshire Reports. RSA 651:5, XV forbids it absolutely, and a published opinion is a permanent and searchable artifact no amount of trial-court relief will reach.

tracks.legalName: Expungement of Records of Arrests and Charges Not Resulting in Conviction (N.J.S.A. 2C:52-6)
tracks.publicName: Expunge a New Jersey arrest that did not lead to a conviction
tracks.mechanism: Records of an arrest, charge and related proceedings that did not result in conviction may be expunged at any time, with no waiting period. Where the case was dismissed or the person was acquitted on all counts, New Jersey Courts states that the court can order an immediate expungement. There is no filing fee. Expungement in New Jersey is defined at N.J.S.A. 2C:52-1 as the extraction and isolation of criminal justice records, not their destruction. In most contexts the person may then answer that the event did not occur. Certain law enforcement, judicial and specified licensing uses survive under N.J.S.A. 2C:52-27. The relief reaches New Jersey records only: federal and out-of-state records are untouched, although out-of-state convictions still count when assessing eligibility. There is no federal immigration effect.
exclusions: Title 39 motor vehicle matters, including DWI. N.J.S.A. 2C:52-28 puts the whole chapter outside them.
Federal, out-of-state and tribal records.
A dismissal following completion of a supervisory treatment or diversion programme, which is treated differently and interacts with the one-time-only rules elsewhere in the chapter.

waitingPeriods.condition: Arrest or charge not resulting in conviction
waitingPeriods.duration: none. Relief is available at any time, and an immediate expungement is available where the case was dismissed or the person acquitted on all counts

tracks.legalName: Expungement of an Indictable Conviction (N.J.S.A. 2C:52-2)
tracks.publicName: Expunge a New Jersey felony conviction
tracks.mechanism: "Indictable offence" is New Jersey's word for a felony and is heard in Superior Court; "disorderly persons" and "petty disorderly persons" offences are the misdemeanour equivalents and are usually Municipal Court matters. An expungement application may be presented where the person has one crime conviction and no subsequent crime conviction; or one crime and no more than three disorderly persons or petty disorderly persons offences; or multiple convictions all listed in a single judgment of conviction; or multiple convictions that were interdependent or closely related in circumstances and committed as part of a sequence of events within a comparatively short period, regardless of the individual conviction or sentencing dates. The single-judgment and closely-related routes carry no numeric cap, which is the difference between a five-year petition and a ten-year Clean Slate petition for a participant with several convictions from one episode. The ordinary waiting period is five years from the latest of the most recent conviction, payment of any court-ordered financial assessment, satisfactory completion of probation or parole, or release from incarceration. Expungement in New Jersey is defined at N.J.S.A. 2C:52-1 as the extraction and isolation of criminal justice records, not their destruction. In most contexts the person may then answer that the event did not occur. Certain law enforcement, judicial and specified licensing uses survive under N.J.S.A. 2C:52-27. The relief reaches New Jersey records only: federal and out-of-state records are untouched, although out-of-state convictions still count when assessing eligibility. There is no federal immigration effect.
exclusions: Any conviction on the non-expungeable lists at N.J.S.A. 2C:52-2(b) and (c), which cover criminal homicide other than certain death by auto, kidnapping, luring and enticing, human trafficking, aggravated sexual assault and sexual assault and most sex offences, endangering the welfare of a child by sexual conduct, robbery, arson, perjury and false swearing, offences against public officials or government, official misconduct and bribery and public corruption by a public officer or employee, and drug distribution above the statutory thresholds. A single non-expungeable conviction defeats both this track and Clean Slate. The lists have not been read line by line and remain a build blocker.
Title 39 motor vehicle matters, including DWI. N.J.S.A. 2C:52-28.
A further petition after a previous criminal conviction expungement, barred by N.J.S.A. 2C:52-14(e), except that Clean Slate remains available.
Federal, out-of-state and tribal records, which are not reachable but do count toward eligibility.

waitingPeriods.condition: Ordinary route, measured from the latest of the most recent conviction, payment of any court-ordered financial assessment, satisfactory completion of probation or parole, or release from incarceration
waitingPeriods.duration: 5 years

waitingPeriods.condition: Early pathway: the court-ordered financial assessment is satisfied but less than five years have expired from the date of satisfaction, the five-year requirement is otherwise met, and the person substantially complied with a payment plan or could not do so due to compelling circumstances affecting ability to pay
waitingPeriods.duration: less than 5 years, on a compelling-circumstances finding

waitingPeriods.condition: Early pathway: at least four but less than five years have expired from the latest sentence event, with no intervening conviction, and the court finds compelling circumstances. N.J.S.A. 2C:52-2(a)(2)
waitingPeriods.duration: at least 4 but less than 5 years

waitingPeriods.condition: Unpaid financial assessment subject to the comprehensive enforcement programme, unsatisfied for reasons other than willful noncompliance, where the five-year requirement is otherwise met. waitingPeriods.duration: 5 years, with the balance converted rather than blocking

generationRequirements.question: What is your full legal name, and have you used any other names?
What is your date of birth?
Do you know your New Jersey State Bureau of Identification (SBI) number?
generationRequirements.conditionDescription: Asked because the petition and the criminal history request both use it. If the participant does not know it, the SBI history supplies it.

generationRequirements.question: Which New Jersey county do you live in?
generationRequirements.conditionDescription: Asked because venue is the county of residence or a county where a conviction was adjudged, and the participant may choose.

generationRequirements.question: For each matter: the county, the court and its level, the complaint or indictment number, the docket number, the arrest date, the offence and statute, the disposition and its date.
generationRequirements.conditionDescription: Asked because missing case identifiers are the leading cause of rejected petitions.

generationRequirements.question: List every conviction you have anywhere, including other states and federal court, with the grading and the date.
generationRequirements.conditionDescription: Asked because out-of-state and federal convictions cannot be expunged here but do count toward eligibility and toward the offence counts.

generationRequirements.question: Is any charge pending against you now, anywhere?
Have you ever had a New Jersey record expunged before?
generationRequirements.conditionDescription: Asked because N.J.S.A. 2C:52-14(e) bars a further petition after a previous criminal conviction expungement, except on the Clean Slate route.

generationRequirements.question: Were any of these matters resolved through pretrial intervention, conditional discharge or another diversion programme?
generationRequirements.conditionDescription: Asked because a dismissal after diversion is treated differently from an ordinary dismissal and the participant will describe both as a dismissal.

generationRequirements.question: Were any of these matters motor vehicle charges, including DWI?
generationRequirements.conditionDescription: Asked as a hard screen: N.J.S.A. 2C:52-28 puts Title 39 motor vehicle matters outside the expungement chapter entirely, so a DWI cannot be expunged and the participant must be told so rather than sold a petition.

generationRequirements.question: Have you paid every fine, fee, penalty and restitution ordered in these cases, and if not, why not?
generationRequirements.conditionDescription: Asked because the waiting period runs from final payment, and because an unpaid assessment that is unpaid for reasons other than willful noncompliance does not necessarily stop the application.

generationRequirements.question: When did you finish probation or parole, or get released from custody, on each matter?
For each conviction, was it an indictable offence, a disorderly persons offence, or a petty disorderly persons offence?
generationRequirements.conditionDescription: Asked because the count drives the route, and answered from the official record rather than recollection.

generationRequirements.question: Were any of these convictions entered in a single judgment of conviction, or on the same day?
generationRequirements.conditionDescription: Asked because that route carries no numeric cap.

generationRequirements.question: Did any of these offences happen as part of one connected sequence of events over a short period?
generationRequirements.conditionDescription: Asked because the interdependent-or-closely-related route also carries no numeric cap, and characterising it is where the largest eligibility payoff sits.

generationRequirements.question: Did any conviction involve marijuana or hashish, or drug paraphernalia used with them?
generationRequirements.conditionDescription: Asked because the regrading rules in the statute treat specified marijuana and hashish convictions as disorderly persons offences rather than crimes, and treat specified possession, use, under-the-influence and paraphernalia convictions as not convictions at all, which can move the participant between routes or from ineligible to eligible.

generationRequirements.question: Was any conviction a third or fourth degree controlled dangerous substance crime?
generationRequirements.conditionDescription: Asked because N.J.S.A. 2C:52-2(c)(3) permits expungement of certain such crimes on a showing of compelling circumstances, and the Judiciary kit has a dedicated checkbox for it. The showing itself is not template output.

tracks.legalName: Expungement of Disorderly Persons and Petty Disorderly Persons Offences (N.J.S.A. 2C:52-3)
tracks.publicName: Expunge New Jersey disorderly persons offences
tracks.mechanism: Available to a person convicted of one or more disorderly persons or petty disorderly persons offences who has not been convicted of any crime, in this State or any other jurisdiction; a person with any crime conviction uses N.J.S.A. 2C:52-2 instead. Three alternative routes: no more than five disorderly persons offences, no more than five petty disorderly persons offences, or a combination of no more than five; or multiple offences whose convictions were entered on the same day; or multiple offences that were interdependent or closely related in circumstances and committed as part of a sequence of events within a comparatively short period. The same-day and closely-related routes carry no numeric cap. The statute expressly provides that a person shall not be required to provide plea or sentencing transcripts or presentence reports with the application or any other filing. Expungement in New Jersey is defined at N.J.S.A. 2C:52-1 as the extraction and isolation of criminal justice records, not their destruction. In most contexts the person may then answer that the event did not occur. Certain law enforcement, judicial and specified licensing uses survive under N.J.S.A. 2C:52-27. The relief reaches New Jersey records only: federal and out-of-state records are untouched, although out-of-state convictions still count when assessing eligibility. There is no federal immigration effect.
exclusions: Any crime conviction anywhere, which moves the participant to the indictable track.
Title 39 motor vehicle matters, including DWI. N.J.S.A. 2C:52-28.
A further petition after a previous criminal conviction expungement, barred by N.J.S.A. 2C:52-14(e), except that Clean Slate remains available.
Federal, out-of-state and tribal records, which are not reachable but do count toward eligibility.

waitingPeriods.condition: Ordinary route, measured from the latest of the most recent conviction, payment of any court-ordered financial assessment, satisfactory completion of probation or parole, or release from incarceration
waitingPeriods.duration: 5 years

waitingPeriods.condition: Early pathway: the financial assessment is satisfied but less than five years have expired since satisfaction, the five-year requirement is otherwise met, and there was substantial compliance with a payment plan or compelling circumstances affecting ability to pay
waitingPeriods.duration: less than 5 years, on a compelling-circumstances finding

waitingPeriods.condition: Early pathway: at least three but less than five years have expired from the latest sentence event, with no intervening conviction of any grade, and the court finds compelling circumstances. N.J.S.A. 2C:52-3(b)(2)
waitingPeriods.duration: at least 3 but less than 5 years

waitingPeriods.condition: Unpaid financial assessment subject to the comprehensive enforcement programme, unsatisfied for reasons other than willful noncompliance, where the five-year requirement is otherwise met. The court may grant and enter a civil judgment for the unpaid portion in the name of the Treasurer under N.J.S.A. 2C:52-23.1
waitingPeriods.duration: 5 years, with the balance converted rather than blocking

tracks.legalName: "Clean Slate" Expungement by Petition (N.J.S.A. 2C:52-5.3)
tracks.publicName: Clear your whole New Jersey record after ten years
tracks.mechanism: A person convicted of one or more crimes, one or more disorderly persons or petty disorderly persons offences, or any combination, who is not otherwise eligible under another section, may petition to expunge the entire record, unless the person has a conviction for a crime not subject to expungement under N.J.S.A. 2C:52-2(b) or (c). The waiting period is ten years from the latest of the most recent conviction, payment of any court-ordered financial assessment, satisfactory completion of probation or parole, or release from incarceration. Where the ten-year period is otherwise satisfied but a financial assessment is unpaid for reasons other than willful noncompliance, the person may still apply and the balance is converted to a civil judgment transferred to the State Treasurer. The route is available notwithstanding the N.J.S.A. 2C:52-14(e) prior-expungement bar. No application may be filed under this section after the automated Clean Slate process is established. Expungement in New Jersey is defined at N.J.S.A. 2C:52-1 as the extraction and isolation of criminal justice records, not their destruction. In most contexts the person may then answer that the event did not occur. Certain law enforcement, judicial and specified licensing uses survive under N.J.S.A. 2C:52-27. The relief reaches New Jersey records only: federal and out-of-state records are untouched, although out-of-state convictions still count when assessing eligibility. There is no federal immigration effect.
exclusions: Any conviction for a crime not subject to expungement under N.J.S.A. 2C:52-2(b) or (c). One such conviction defeats the track entirely.
A person who is otherwise eligible under another section. Whether "not otherwise eligible" is applied strictly is recorded below as an open question.
Title 39 motor vehicle matters, including DWI.
Federal, out-of-state and tribal records, which are not reachable but do count toward eligibility.

tracks.legalName: Automated "Clean Slate" Process (N.J.S.A. 2C:52-5.4)
tracks.publicName: New Jersey's automatic record clearing, and where it stands
tracks.mechanism: The State shall develop and implement an automated process by which all convictions and related records are rendered inaccessible to the public, through sealing, expungement or an equivalent process, for a person convicted of one or more crimes or offences, unless the person has a conviction not subject to expungement under N.J.S.A. 2C:52-2(b) or (c), upon the expiration of ten years. A task force was established to design it and reported in 2022. The process is not operational: Assembly Bill A5095, introduced May 14, 2026, states that it still does not exist and that eligible people must still file a petition with the court. The section also requires that a person's convictions and criminal history be restored in certain circumstances if the person is subsequently convicted of a crime not subject to expungement. Expungement in New Jersey is defined at N.J.S.A. 2C:52-1 as the extraction and isolation of criminal justice records, not their destruction. In most contexts the person may then answer that the event did not occur. Certain law enforcement, judicial and specified licensing uses survive under N.J.S.A. 2C:52-27. The relief reaches New Jersey records only: federal and out-of-state records are untouched, although out-of-state convictions still count when assessing eligibility. There is no federal immigration effect.
exclusions: Any conviction for a crime not subject to expungement under N.J.S.A. 2C:52-2(b) or (c).
Everyone, for the time being. The process is not operational as of 2026-08-06 and nothing happens automatically.

tracks.legalName: Petition to Expunge Arrest Records and Public Records upon Identity Theft (NMSA 1978, Section 29-3A-3)
tracks.publicName: Clear a New Mexico record that is not yours
tracks.mechanism: A person wrongfully identified in arrest records or public records as a result of identity theft may petition the district court to expunge those records. On a showing that the person is a victim of identity theft the court shall order expungement and cause the order to be delivered to all relevant law enforcement agencies and courts. The proceeding is a civil petition in district court even where the underlying case was in municipal, magistrate or metropolitan court. Rule 1-077.1 supplies the procedure and its use of Form 4-951 is mandatory; the rule and every form in the set were amended by Supreme Court Order No. S-1-RCR-2024-00099, effective for all cases pending or filed on or after December 31, 2025.
exclusions: Records of another state, and federal, tribal and military records. A New Mexico district court cannot reach them.

Driving while intoxicated citations maintained by the taxation and revenue department, computer-aided dispatch information and log books relating to breath alcohol testing equipment, which Section 29-3A-2(A) excludes from the definition of arrest records.

The categories Section 29-3A-2(C) carves out of public records, including confidential arrest-record information, a district attorney or attorney general law-enforcement file, certain children, youth and families department, human services department and public education department records, and a record received through an authorized background check.

waitingPeriods.condition: None. Section 29-3A-3 imposes no waiting period for identity-theft expungement

tracks.legalName: Petition to Expunge Arrest Records and Public Records upon Release Without Conviction (NMSA 1978, Section 29-3A-4)
tracks.publicName: Expunge a New Mexico case that did not end in a conviction
tracks.mechanism: One year from the date of final disposition, a person released without conviction may petition the district court where the charges originated to expunge the arrest records and public records of that case. Relief is mandatory on the findings: if the court finds no other charge or proceeding is pending and that the petitioner was released without conviction, it must order expungement. The petition is filed under seal under Rule 1-079 NMRA. Two responding parties are served by first-class mail and have sixty days to object or file a notice of non-objection; after that window the petitioner must file a notice of completion of briefing with an affirmation attached before any hearing on the merits will be set, and where no objection is filed the court may decide on the pleadings and affirmation without a hearing.
exclusions: Any case in which a conviction was entered. That is the conviction track under Section 29-3A-5.
Cases where another charge or proceeding is pending against the petitioner. The court must find there is none.
Records of another state, and federal, tribal and military records.

Driving while intoxicated citations maintained by the taxation and revenue department, computer-aided dispatch information and log books relating to breath alcohol testing equipment, which Section 29-3A-2(A) excludes from arrest records. A successful expungement on this track therefore leaves some DWI-related records untouched.
The categories Section 29-3A-2(C) carves out of public records.

releaseBlockers.question: Whether an arrest that never became a filed court case requires its own petition. The Judiciary instruction packet says a separate petition is needed for arrests not associated with a filed case, while Rule 1-077.1(B)(4) NMRA, as renumbered effective December 31, 2025, permits one petition to cover any number of arrests, criminal charges filed without arrest and convictions within a single judicial district. The rule text was read on 2026-08-06 and expressly contemplates charges filed without arrest, but the instruction packet has not been reconciled to it.

tracks.legalName: Petition to Expunge Arrest Records and Public Records upon Conviction (NMSA 1978, Section 29-3A-5)
tracks.publicName: Expunge a New Mexico conviction
tracks.mechanism: A person convicted of a municipal ordinance violation, misdemeanor or felony may, after completing the sentence and paying any fines or fees owed to the state for that conviction, petition the district court in the county of conviction to expunge the arrest records and public records related to it. Relief is discretionary. The court must find no other charge or proceeding pending, that justice will be served, that victim restitution ordered in connection with the conviction has been fulfilled, and that no other criminal conviction has occurred during a waiting period of two to ten years measured by offence class from the last date the petitioner completed a sentence in any jurisdiction. Five categories of offence are excluded outright. Three responding parties are served, the objection window is sixty days, the notice of completion of briefing must be filed before any hearing, and Rule 1-077.1(J) NMRA requires a hearing on this track in every case.
exclusions: An offense committed against a child. Section 29-3A-5(G).
An offense that caused great bodily harm or death to another person. Section 29-3A-5(G).
A sex offense as defined in Section 29-11A-3 NMSA 1978. Section 29-3A-5(G).
Embezzlement under Section 30-16-8 NMSA 1978. Section 29-3A-5(G).
An offense involving driving while under the influence of intoxicating liquor or drugs. Section 29-3A-5(G).
Any conviction where the sentence has not been completed, or where fines or fees owed to the state for that conviction are unpaid. Section 29-3A-5(A).
Any case where another charge or proceeding is pending against the petitioner anywhere.

Any case where the petitioner has another criminal conviction within the applicable waiting period, measured from the last date on which they completed a sentence for a conviction in any jurisdiction.
Records of another state, and federal, tribal and military records.

waitingPeriods.condition: Conviction for a municipal ordinance violation, or a misdemeanor not otherwise listed, with no other criminal conviction in the period. Section 29-3A-5(C)(4)(a)
waitingPeriods.duration: 2 years measured from the last date the petitioner completed a sentence for a conviction in any jurisdiction

waitingPeriods.condition: Misdemeanor conviction for aggravated battery under Section 30-3-5(B), or a fourth degree felony not otherwise listed. Section 29-3A-5(C)(4)(b)
waitingPeriods.duration: 4 years measured from the last date the petitioner completed a sentence for a conviction in any jurisdiction

waitingPeriods.condition: Third degree felony not otherwise listed. Section 29-3A-5(C)(4)(c)
waitingPeriods.duration: 6 years measured from the last date the petitioner completed a sentence for a conviction in any jurisdiction

waitingPeriods.condition: Second degree felony not otherwise listed. Section 29-3A-5(C)(4)(d)
waitingPeriods.duration: 8 years measured from the last date the petitioner completed a sentence for a conviction in any jurisdiction

waitingPeriods.condition: First degree felony, or any offense under the Crimes Against Household Members Act, Sections 30-3-10 to 30-3-18. Section 29-3A-5(C)(4)(e)
waitingPeriods.duration: 10 years measured from the last date the petitioner completed a sentence for a conviction in any jurisdiction

tracks.venue: Rule 1-077.1(B)(3) NMRA: the district court in the county in which the petitioner's conviction was entered.

destination.name: New Mexico district court for the county in which the conviction was entered
destination.detail: A civil petition filed with the district court clerk. It is not filed under seal, and if it is combined with a release-without-conviction request the whole filing is treated as a conviction petition and loses the Rule 1-079 NMRA seal. Copies are mailed by first-class United States mail to the district attorney for the county where the conviction was entered, to the New Mexico Department of Public Safety at P.O. Box 1628, Santa Fe, New Mexico 87504-1628, and to the law enforcement agency that arrested the petitioner, and a certificate of service on Form 4-956 NMRA is filed with the court.

participantActionRequired.description: Obtain FBI Identity History Summary. Request an Identity History Summary from the FBI and pay the FBI's fee. It must be dated no later than ninety days before the petition is filed, so order it once the rest of the packet is nearly ready. Form 4-953 paragraph 16 requires it alongside the DPS sheet.
participantActionRequired.obtainedFrom: Federal Bureau of Investigation

participantActionRequired.description: Check your answer to "For each conviction, what are the case number, the court, the arresting agency, the charge and the date?" against FBI Identity History Summary, and correct the packet if they disagree.

Obtain New Mexico Department of Public Safety Record of Arrest and Prosecution (RAP) sheet. Complete the DPS Authorization for Release of Information, have it notarized with an original signature, and send it to DPS with a $15.00 money order or cashier's check per record check. It must be dated no later than ninety days before filing.
participantActionRequired.obtainedFrom: New Mexico Department of Public Safety

participantActionRequired.description: Check your answer to "For each conviction, what are the case number, the court, the arresting agency, the charge and the date?" against New Mexico Department of Public Safety Record of Arrest and Prosecution (RAP) sheet, and correct the packet if they disagree.

Obtain Judgment and sentence, and proof that the sentence was completed. Ask the clerk of the court that entered the conviction for the judgment and sentence, and ask probation or parole for a discharge document. Form 4-953 paragraph 17(a) asks for documentation showing completion of the sentences for the convictions you are seeking to expunge.
participantActionRequired.obtainedFrom: The court that entered the conviction, and probation or parole

participantActionRequired.description: Check your answer to "On what date did you finish the sentence for each conviction, including any probation or parole?" against Judgment and sentence, and proof that the sentence was completed, and correct the packet if they disagree.

Obtain Proof that sentences for any other convictions were completed. Form 4-953 paragraph 17(b) asks for documentation showing completion of sentences for any other convictions served. Because the waiting period runs from the most recent sentence completed in any jurisdiction, gather this for out-of-state convictions too.
participantActionRequired.obtainedFrom: Each court, probation or parole authority that handled those convictions, in any jurisdiction
participantActionRequired.conditionDescription: Where the participant has served any other sentence, including in another state.

participantActionRequired.description: Check your answer to "Have you completed a sentence for any conviction in any other state, or in a federal, tribal or military court — and if so, when did the most recent one end?" against Proof that sentences for any other convictions were completed, and correct the packet if they disagree.
participantActionRequired.conditionDescription: Where the participant has served any other sentence, including in another state.

participantActionRequired.description: Obtain Proof of final payment of fines and fees. Ask the clerk or the collections office for a receipt or a zero-balance statement for the conviction you want cleared. Form 4-953 paragraph 17(c) asks for it.
participantActionRequired.obtainedFrom: The court or agency that collected them

participantActionRequired.description: Check your answer to "Have you paid all fines and fees owed for the conviction you want cleared, and on what date was the final payment made?" against Proof of final payment of fines and fees, and correct the packet if they disagree.

Obtain Proof that victim restitution was completed. Ask the court or the restitution administrator for a document showing restitution was paid in full. Form 4-953 paragraph 17(d) asks for it and Section 29-3A-5(C)(3) makes it a finding the court must make.
participantActionRequired.obtainedFrom: The court or the agency that administered restitution
participantActionRequired.conditionDescription: Where restitution was ordered in connection with the conviction.

participantActionRequired.description: Check your answer to "Was victim restitution ordered in connection with the conviction, and have you finished paying it?" against Proof that victim restitution was completed, and correct the packet if they disagree.
participantActionRequired.conditionDescription: Where restitution was ordered in connection with the conviction.

tracks.legalName: Automatic Expungement of Cannabis Arrest and Conviction Records, and the Administrative Office of the Courts Verification and Expedited-Request Procedure (NMSA 1978, Section 29-3A-8)
tracks.publicName: New Mexico cannabis record clearing
tracks.mechanism: Where a person was charged with a cannabis offence that is no longer a crime on June 29, 2021, or that would have resulted in a lesser offence had the Cannabis Regulation Act been in effect, all public records held by a court or a state or local agency relating to the arrest or conviction are automatically expunged two years after the conviction date, or two years after the arrest date if there was no conviction. For a person under eighteen at the time, the records are retained for two years or until they turn eighteen, whichever comes first, and are then automatically expunged. Automatic expungement applies to public records involving only cannabis and cannabis paraphernalia charges and requires destruction of the records. The Administrative Office of the Courts must implement a procedure allowing eligible people to verify whether automatic expungement has occurred and to request expedited automatic expungement where it has not; where an arrest or conviction involved cannabis and non-cannabis charges, the person may request expungement of the eligible cannabis charges through that same AOC procedure. Requests to the AOC remain confidential and are not subject to disclosure. There is no court petition on this track: Rule 1-077.1(A) NMRA now excepts cannabis records from the expungement rule, former Rule 1-077.1(B)(4) was deleted and Form 4-954 NMRA was withdrawn, all effective December 31, 2025.
authority: Cannabis Regulation Act, NMSA 1978, Sections 26-2C-1 to 26-2C-42
exclusions: Any offence that is still a crime under the Cannabis Regulation Act and would not have resulted in a lesser offence had that Act been in effect.
Records of another state, and federal, tribal and military records.
Anyone currently or formerly incarcerated for a cannabis offence who is seeking dismissal, vacatur or redesignation of the sentence. That is Section 29-3A-9 and it is a different track.

Non-cannabis charges within a mixed case. Automatic expungement under Section 29-3A-8(A) applies to public records involving only cannabis and cannabis paraphernalia charges; a mixed case reaches the eligible cannabis charges only through the Section 29-3A-8(C) request to the Administrative Office of the Courts, and the non-cannabis charges are left to the release-without-conviction or conviction track.

tracks.legalName: Dismissal of Sentence, Vacatur and Redesignation for Cannabis Convictions (NMSA 1978, Section 29-3A-9)
tracks.publicName: Cannabis sentences and convictions that may now be invalid
tracks.mechanism: A correctional facility, county jail or juvenile correctional facility holding a person for a cannabis offence that is no longer a crime, or that would have been a lesser offence had the Cannabis Regulation Act been in effect, was required to notify the court that the case may be reopened for dismissal of the sentence or expunged. The court must reopen the case and dismiss the sentence if it is legally invalid. A person who has completed such a sentence is entitled to have the conviction dismissed and expunged as legally invalid, or redesignated as a penalty assessment citation. The Department of Public Safety was to identify potentially eligible past convictions and notify the corrections department, prosecutors and defence counsel, and prosecutors had until July 1, 2022 to decide whether to challenge a dismissal, expungement or redesignation. This is sentence relief and vacatur, not record clearing, and it turns on a legal-invalidity analysis.

tracks.legalName: Petition to Seal Records After Conviction (NRS 179.245)
tracks.publicName: Seal your Nevada conviction
tracks.mechanism: A person convicted in Nevada may petition the court in which they were convicted to seal all records relating to the conviction once the waiting period for the offence category has run. The periods are ten years for a category A felony, a crime of violence or residential burglary; five years for a category B, C or D felony; two years for a category E felony or a gross misdemeanour; seven years for non-felony Medicaid fraud, non-felony DUI or non-felony battery constituting domestic violence; two years for misdemeanour battery, harassment, stalking or a protective-order violation; and one year for any other misdemeanour. The trigger differs by paragraph: paragraphs (a) to (d) run from release from actual custody or discharge from parole or probation, whichever is later, while paragraphs (e) to (g) run from release from actual custody or from the end of a suspended sentence, whichever is later, and the eligibility engine must model both. NRS 179.2445 creates a rebuttable presumption that records should be sealed where the applicant satisfies all statutory requirements, except for a defendant dishonourably discharged from probation under NRS 176A.850, and if the prosecutor stipulates or fails to object within 30 days the court may seal without a hearing. Nevada calls it record sealing and never expungement: the Department of Public Safety states directly that sealing is not expungement because it does not authorise destruction of the records. Under NRS 179.285 the proceedings are deemed never to have occurred and civil rights are restored, but NRS 179.295 allows sealed records to be reopened and NRS 179.301 allows certain persons and agencies to inspect them. A Nevada order does not bind out-of-state or federal agencies and does not reach records they hold. Sealing does not restore firearm rights; only a pardon that does not restrict the right to bear arms does.
exclusions: A crime against a child as defined in NRS 179D.0357. NRS 179.245(6).
A sexual offence as defined in NRS 179.245(10)(b), which is an eighteen-item enumerated list. NRS 179.245(6).
Invasion of the home with a deadly weapon under NRS 205.067. NRS 179.245(6).
DUI under NRS 484C.110 or 484C.120 punishable as a felony under NRS 484C.400(1)(c), subject to the NRS 179.245(7) carve-back.
A violation of NRS 484C.430, and a homicide resulting from DUI or from conduct prohibited by NRS 484C.110, 484C.130 or 484C.430.
A violation of NRS 488.410 punishable as a felony under NRS 488.427, and violations of NRS 488.420 or 488.425.
Any case where the petitioner was charged with a pending offence, or convicted of any offence other than a minor moving or standing traffic violation, during the prescribed period. NRS 179.245(5).

destination.name: The district attorney's or city attorney's office first, then the clerk of the appropriate court
destination.detail: Nevada's workflow puts the prosecutor in the middle rather than at the end: the state's own instructions direct the petitioner to prepare the petition and order, submit them to the prosecuting agency with attachments, and file with the court clerk only after the prosecutor stipulates. Local practice is material. The Clark County District Attorney will not stipulate to petitions that include municipal court arrests or convictions, so a packet covering both must go to the appropriate city attorney and then to the district attorney, with a separate signature line for each prosecuting agency on the order. Only one petition, affidavit and order is required to seal all records within Clark County, and justice court petitions must be captioned to the specific township. Las Vegas Municipal Court requires its own Petition, Declaration and Verification, Order and Stipulation and denies typed signatures outright. Reno Municipal Court charges a filing fee, sets the petition for hearing at least 60 days after filing, and applies the sex trafficking fee exemption.

tracks.legalName: Petition to Seal Records After Dismissal, Declination of Prosecution or Acquittal (NRS 179.255(1))
tracks.publicName: Seal a Nevada arrest that did not end in a conviction
tracks.mechanism: Where charges were dismissed the petition may be filed at any time after the dismissal; where prosecution was declined it may be filed at any time after the applicable statute of limitations has run, or any time eight years after the arrest, or pursuant to a stipulation between the parties; and where the person was acquitted it may be filed at any time after the acquittal. On an acquittal, and a finding that there is no evidence further action will be brought, the court shall order the records sealed, so relief is mandatory there; on a dismissal or declination it is discretionary but carries the NRS 179.2445 presumption. The NRS 179.245(6) conviction exclusions do not govern this track, so an arrest for an offence that could never be sealed as a conviction is still sealable where the case was dismissed or ended in acquittal. NRS 179.255(3)(b) adds an express requirement that the petition state the disposition of the proceedings. Nevada calls it record sealing and never expungement: the Department of Public Safety states directly that sealing is not expungement because it does not authorise destruction of the records. Under NRS 179.285 the proceedings are deemed never to have occurred and civil rights are restored, but NRS 179.295 allows sealed records to be reopened and NRS 179.301 allows certain persons and agencies to inspect them. A Nevada order does not bind out-of-state or federal agencies and does not reach records they hold. Sealing does not restore firearm rights; only a pardon that does not restrict the right to bear arms does.
exclusions: None stated in NRS 179.255. The NRS 179.245(6) exclusion list governs convictions and must not be allowed to leak into this track.
Any case where there is evidence that further action will be brought against the person.

tracks.legalName: Consolidated Petition to Seal More Than One Record in District Court (NRS 179.2595)
tracks.publicName: Seal several Nevada records in one filing
tracks.mechanism: NRS 179.2595 permits a person seeking to seal more than one record to petition the district court for the county, which may seal all the records within that county including justice and municipal court cases. This is a venue overlay on the conviction and non-conviction tracks rather than a separate remedy: each underlying record still has to satisfy its own section. Clark County practice illustrates both the value and the trap: only one petition, affidavit and order is required to seal all records within the county, but the district attorney will not stipulate to petitions that include municipal court matters, so the packet must go to the appropriate city attorney and then to the district attorney with a separate signature line for each prosecuting agency. Nevada calls it record sealing and never expungement: the Department of Public Safety states directly that sealing is not expungement because it does not authorise destruction of the records. Under NRS 179.285 the proceedings are deemed never to have occurred and civil rights are restored, but NRS 179.295 allows sealed records to be reopened and NRS 179.301 allows certain persons and agencies to inspect them. A Nevada order does not bind out-of-state or federal agencies and does not reach records they hold. Sealing does not restore firearm rights; only a pardon that does not restrict the right to bear arms does.
exclusions: Records in more than one county, which need separate petitions in each county's district court.

tracks.legalName: Sealing of Records After an Unconditional Pardon (NRS 179.273)
tracks.publicName: Seal a Nevada record after a pardon
tracks.mechanism: NRS 179.273 is titled "Sealing of records after unconditional pardon: Automatic sealing; petition; no fee" in the chapter index published by the Nevada Legislature, and the controlling review describes it as providing automatic sealing together with a no-fee petition route. The internal reference omits the section entirely, which the review records as one of its five substantive gaps. Because sealing is automatic in the first instance, the correct first move is verification rather than a filing; the petition exists for the case where the automatic sealing has not happened, and it carries no fee. Nevada calls it record sealing and never expungement: the Department of Public Safety states directly that sealing is not expungement because it does not authorise destruction of the records. Under NRS 179.285 the proceedings are deemed never to have occurred and civil rights are restored, but NRS 179.295 allows sealed records to be reopened and NRS 179.301 allows certain persons and agencies to inspect them. A Nevada order does not bind out-of-state or federal agencies and does not reach records they hold. Sealing does not restore firearm rights; only a pardon that does not restrict the right to bear arms does.
exclusions: A conditional pardon, or any pardon short of an unconditional one, which the section does not reach.
Anyone who does not yet hold a pardon. Applying for one is a Board of Pardons matter and is out of scope.

waitingPeriods.duration: none. The section provides automatic sealing, with a no-fee petition available where it has not occurred

tracks.legalName: Sealing of Records After Decriminalization of an Offence (NRS 179.271)
tracks.publicName: Seal a Nevada record for something that is no longer a crime
tracks.mechanism: NRS 179.271, "Sealing of records after decriminalization of offense", provides a route where the conduct underlying a Nevada record is no longer a crime. The controlling review records the instrument as a written request rather than a full petition and classifies the track as custom_pleading on that basis. The section's presence and official title were confirmed in the chapter index at the Nevada Legislature; its text was not reproduced in the review. Nevada calls it record sealing and never expungement: the Department of Public Safety states directly that sealing is not expungement because it does not authorise destruction of the records. Under NRS 179.285 the proceedings are deemed never to have occurred and civil rights are restored, but NRS 179.295 allows sealed records to be reopened and NRS 179.301 allows certain persons and agencies to inspect them. A Nevada order does not bind out-of-state or federal agencies and does not reach records they hold. Sealing does not restore firearm rights; only a pardon that does not restrict the right to bear arms does.
exclusions: Any offence that remains a crime in Nevada.
Records held outside Nevada, which a Nevada order does not reach.

waitingPeriods.duration: not established by the review beyond the decriminalisation itself

tracks.publicName: Seal a Nevada record after finishing a reentry program

The controlling review approves the track with limitations and treats it as running on the same machinery as the ordinary conviction petition: repository record, generated pleading, prosecutor submission, then filing and service. The section's presence and official title were confirmed in the chapter index at the Nevada Legislature. Nevada calls it record sealing and never expungement: the Department of Public Safety states directly that sealing is not expungement because it does not authorise destruction of the records. Under NRS 179.285 the proceedings are deemed never to have occurred and civil rights are restored, but NRS 179.295 allows sealed records to be reopened and NRS 179.301 allows certain persons and agencies to inspect them. A Nevada order does not bind out-of-state or federal agencies and does not reach records they hold. Sealing does not restore firearm rights; only a pardon that does not restrict the right to bear arms does.
exclusions: Anyone who has not completed the reentry programme.
Records held outside Nevada.

tracks.legalName: Sealing After Dismissal Under a Deferred Judgment (NRS 176.211)
tracks.publicName: Clearing a Nevada case that was dismissed after a deferred judgment
tracks.mechanism: NRS 176.211 governs deferral of judgment and its own sealing. It has now been read in full and the mechanism is settled: sealing is automatic and court-ordered, and there is no participant filing. Under subsection 5, on completion of the terms and conditions and a finding by the court that they have been met, the court discharges the defendant and dismisses the proceedings. Under subsection 6, the court "shall order sealed all documents, papers and exhibits in the defendant's record, minute book entries and entries on dockets, and other documents relating to the case in the custody of such other agencies and officers as are named in the court's order", and "shall order those records sealed without a hearing unless the Division or the prosecutor petitions the court, for good cause shown, not to seal the records and requests a hearing thereon". Subsection 9(a) defines "court" for this section as a district court of the State of Nevada, so a justice court or municipal court matter is not on this route at all. The routing value of the node stands and is now supported rather than assumed: a participant will describe a deferred-judgment dismissal as an ordinary dismissal, and NRS 179.245 expressly excepts NRS 176.211 from the ordinary conviction petition, so sending them to a petition would be the wrong instrument for a remedy they are already entitled to receive without filing anything. Nevada calls it record sealing and never expungement: the Department of Public Safety states directly that sealing is not expungement because it does not authorise destruction of the records. Under NRS 179.285 the proceedings are deemed never to have occurred and civil rights are restored, but NRS 179.295 allows sealed records to be reopened and NRS 179.301 allows certain persons and agencies to inspect them. A Nevada order does not bind out-of-state or federal agencies and does not reach records they hold. Sealing does not restore firearm rights; only a pardon that does not restrict the right to bear arms does.
exclusions: NRS 176.211(7): the court may not order sealing under subsection 6 for a defendant who is charged with a violation of NRS 200.5099 (abuse, neglect, exploitation, isolation or abandonment of an older person or a vulnerable person) and who is discharged under the section. The deferral itself remains available; only the sealing is withheld.

Upstream, NRS 176.211(3)(b) bars deferral of judgment altogether for a defendant convicted of a violent or sexual offense as defined in NRS 202.876, a crime against a child as defined in NRS 179D.0357, a violation of NRS 200.508, or a violation of NRS 574.100 punishable under subsection 6 of that section. A person in any of those categories never reaches this route.
NRS 176.211(9)(a) confines the section to a district court of the State of Nevada. A deferral-like disposition in a justice court or a municipal court is not governed by this section.
Sealing under this section is not available where the deferral was terminated for violation of a term or condition and a judgment of conviction was entered under NRS 176.211(4).
