tracks.legalName: Sealing After a Treatment-Program Discharge, Conditional Dismissal or Set-Aside (NRS 176A.245, 176A.265 and 176A.295)
tracks.publicName: Clearing a Nevada case after a court treatment programme, a conditional dismissal or a set-aside
tracks.mechanism: All three sections have now been read in full and they are structurally identical, differing only in the programme they attach to: NRS 176A.245 to the programme of treatment for alcohol or other substance use under NRS 176A.240, NRS 176A.265 to the programme for treatment of mental illness or intellectual disabilities under NRS 176A.260, and NRS 176A.295 to the programme for treatment of veterans and members of the military under NRS 176A.290. Each has two mechanisms, not one. Subsection 1 is automatic: after the defendant is discharged from probation or the case is dismissed under the corresponding programme section, the justice court, municipal court or district court, as applicable, "shall order sealed" the record if the defendant fulfilled the terms and conditions imposed by the court and the Division, and "shall order those records sealed without a hearing unless the Division petitions the court, for good cause shown, not to seal the records and requests a hearing thereon". Subsection 2 is not automatic: where the defendant was charged with a violation of NRS 200.485, NRS 484C.110 or NRS 484C.120 and the charges were conditionally dismissed or the judgment of conviction set aside, sealing follows only "not sooner than 7 years after" and "upon the filing of a petition by the defendant". So a participant filing does exist on this track, on a defined branch, with a defined waiting period. Subsection 3 of each section bars sealing where the defendant was charged with a violation of NRS 200.508 or NRS 200.5099. Subsection 4 requires the court to send a copy of the order to each agency or officer named in it, each of which must notify the court in writing of compliance. The grouping of the three sections into one track remains correct because the participant cannot be expected to know which programme section their case ran under, and the discharge-type screen remains load-bearing: NRS 179.2445(2) provides that the rebuttable presumption in favour of sealing does not apply to a defendant given a dishonorable discharge from probation under NRS 176A.850, which changes what that participant should expect on the ordinary conviction track. Nevada calls it record sealing and never expungement: the Department of Public Safety states directly that sealing is not expungement because it does not authorise destruction of the records. Under NRS 179.285 the proceedings are deemed never to have occurred and civil rights are restored, but NRS 179.295 allows sealed records to be reopened and NRS 179.301 allows certain persons and agencies to inspect them. A Nevada order does not bind out-of-state or federal agencies and does not reach records they hold. Sealing does not restore firearm rights; only a pardon that does not restrict the right to bear arms does.
exclusions: Subsection 3 of each of NRS 176A.245, 176A.265 and 176A.295: the court may not order sealing under the section where the defendant was charged with a violation of NRS 200.508 (abuse, neglect or endangerment of a child) or NRS 200.5099 (abuse, neglect, exploitation, isolation or abandonment of an older person or a vulnerable person), whether the defendant was discharged from probation, the case was dismissed, or the judgment of conviction was set aside.

The automatic sealing in subsection 1 does not reach a defendant who was charged with a violation of NRS 200.485 (battery constituting domestic violence), NRS 484C.110 or NRS 484C.120 and whose charges were conditionally dismissed or judgment of conviction set aside. Those matters are moved to the subsection 2 branch, which is not automatic and carries a seven-year wait.

The route depends on the case having run through the corresponding chapter 176A programme. A defendant who was never assigned to a programme under NRS 176A.240, NRS 176A.260 or NRS 176A.290 is not on this track.
Sealing under these sections is not available where the defendant failed the programme and was sentenced rather than discharged or dismissed.

tracks.legalName: Removal of a Record from the Central Repository After a Favourable Disposition (NRS 179A.160)
tracks.publicName: Getting a Nevada arrest off the state repository after a favourable outcome
tracks.mechanism: NRS 179A.160 has now been read in full and it is not a route on which nothing is filed. Subsection 1 provides that where a person has been arrested or issued a citation, or has been the subject of a warrant for alleged criminal conduct, and is acquitted or the disposition of the charge is favourable to the person, then "at any time after the charge is dismissed, acquittal is entered or disposition of the charge in favor of the person is final, the person who is the subject of a record of criminal history relating to the arrest, citation or warrant may apply in writing to the Central Repository and the agency which maintains the record to have it removed from the files which are available and generally searched for the purpose of responding to inquiries concerning the criminal history of a person." Subsection 2 makes removal mandatory — "The Central Repository and the agency shall remove the record unless" one of five stated conditions applies. So the participant makes a written application, to two recipients, with no waiting period and no hearing, and the agencies must act unless an exclusion bites. It remains a repository remedy rather than a court sealing order, so it sits alongside the NRS 179.255 petition rather than replacing it, and subsection 3 preserves a court's separate authority to order deletion or modification of a record. Nevada calls it record sealing and never expungement: the Department of Public Safety states directly that sealing is not expungement because it does not authorise destruction of the records, and NRS 179A.160 likewise removes a record from the files that are available and generally searched rather than destroying it. Under NRS 179.285 the proceedings are deemed never to have occurred and civil rights are restored, but NRS 179.295 allows sealed records to be reopened and NRS 179.301 allows certain persons and agencies to inspect them. A Nevada order does not bind out-of-state or federal agencies and does not reach records they hold. Sealing does not restore firearm rights; only a pardon that does not restrict the right to bear arms does.
exclusions: NRS 179A.160(2)(a): the person is a fugitive.
NRS 179A.160(2)(b): the case is under active prosecution according to a current certificate of a prosecuting attorney.

NRS 179A.160(2)(c): the disposition of the case was a deferred prosecution, plea bargain or other similar disposition. This is the exclusion that most often defeats the route in practice and it is why a participant whose case was resolved by a deferral of judgment belongs on the NRS 176.211 track and not here.
NRS 179A.160(2)(d): the person has a prior conviction for a felony or gross misdemeanour in any jurisdiction in the United States — not merely in Nevada.
NRS 179A.160(2)(e): the person has been arrested for or charged with another crime, other than a minor traffic violation, since the arrest, citation or warrant which the person seeks to have removed.

waitingPeriods.condition: None. NRS 179A.160(1) permits the application "at any time after the charge is dismissed, acquittal is entered or disposition of the charge in favor of the person is final". The only temporal condition is that the favourable disposition be final.

destination.name: The Central Repository for Nevada Records of Criminal History, and the agency which maintains the record
destination.detail: NRS 179A.160(1) directs the application to two recipients and not one: the Central Repository for Nevada Records of Criminal History, administered by the Nevada State Police Records, Communications and Compliance Division at 333 West Nye Lane, Suite 100, Carson City, Nevada 89706, and the agency which maintains the record, ordinarily the arresting agency. The application is made in writing by the person who is the subject of the record. It is not a court filing, no order issues on it, and it does not reach the court's own record, which is why the parallel screen for the court sealing petition matters.

tracks.legalName: Sealing of a Case Terminated in the Defendant's Favour (CPL § 160.50)
tracks.publicName: Your New York case that ended in your favor should already be sealed
tracks.mechanism: Where a criminal action terminates in the defendant's favour — a dismissal, an acquittal, a declination to prosecute, an adjournment in contemplation of dismissal that is then dismissed, or a vacated or overturned conviction — the record is sealed by direction of the court at disposition. There is no waiting period, no application and nothing to file. New York seals; it does not expunge, except for the marijuana destruction remedy. A sealed record does not appear on background checks run by employers, housing providers and other non-law-enforcement entities, and the person may generally answer that they have no criminal record. Sealed records remain accessible to law enforcement, prosecutors and courts in a new criminal case; to entities permitted or required to run fingerprint-based background checks for work with children, the elderly and people with disabilities; to entities mandated by law to consider sealed records; to the New York State Education Department for hiring, discipline and licensing; to private transportation network companies; to police and peace officer employers; and for firearms licensing. Federal and immigration authorities may also reach them, and a sealed conviction still counts as a predicate for sentence enhancement in a later case. New York sealing reaches New York State records only.
exclusions: An adjournment in contemplation of dismissal that has not yet been dismissed. The ACD period must run first.
Federal and out-of-state records.
Cases where the prosecutor moved successfully to keep the record unsealed in the interests of justice. The scope of that motion is recorded below as an open question.

tracks.legalName: Clean Slate Automatic Sealing of Criminal Convictions (CPL § 160.57(1)(b))
tracks.publicName: New York Clean Slate
tracks.mechanism: Eligible New York convictions are sealed automatically, with nothing filed. A misdemeanour seals when at least three years have passed from the defendant's release from incarceration, or from the imposition of sentence if there was no sentence of incarceration; a felony seals when at least eight years have passed from the date the defendant was last released from incarceration for the sentence of the conviction eligible for sealing, or from the imposition of sentence if there was no incarceration. If the defendant is subsequently convicted of a crime before a prior conviction is sealed, the calculation of time for that prior conviction starts on the same date as the calculation for the subsequent conviction: a re-anchoring rule, not a pause. Every condition must be satisfied, including that the defendant is not currently under the supervision of any probation or parole department for the conviction eligible for sealing, that no subsequent criminal charge is pending in this state, that the conviction is not for an offence defined as a sex offence or sexually violent offence under Correction Law § 168-a, and that it is not a class A felony, except that class A felony offences defined in Penal Law article 220 are carved back in. New York seals; it does not expunge, except for the marijuana destruction remedy. A sealed record does not appear on background checks run by employers, housing providers and other non-law-enforcement entities, and the person may generally answer that they have no criminal record. Sealed records remain accessible to law enforcement, prosecutors and courts in a new criminal case; to entities permitted or required to run fingerprint-based background checks for work with children, the elderly and people with disabilities; to entities mandated by law to consider sealed records; to the New York State Education Department for hiring, discipline and licensing; to private transportation network companies; to police and peace officer employers; and for firearms licensing. Federal and immigration authorities may also reach them, and a sealed conviction still counts as a predicate for sentence enhancement in a later case. New York sealing reaches New York State records only.
exclusions: Convictions for an offence defined as a sex offence or a sexually violent offence under Correction Law § 168-a.

Class A felony convictions, except class A felony offences defined in Penal Law article 220, which are carved back in. This is the opposite of the CPL § 160.59 list, which excludes all class A felonies including drug felonies.
Any conviction where the defendant is currently under the supervision of a probation or parole department for that conviction.
Any conviction where a subsequent criminal charge is pending in New York.
Federal and out-of-state convictions, which New York sealing does not reach.

tracks.legalName: Marijuana Conviction Expungement and Destruction under the Marihuana Regulation and Taxation Act, with CPL § 160.50
tracks.publicName: New York marijuana records are actually destroyed
tracks.mechanism: Convictions for the marijuana offences described in CPL § 160.50(3)(k) are vacated, dismissed and expunged by operation of law under § 160.50(5)(a). That stage is automatic: there is no waiting period, no motion, no fee and nothing for the participant to file, and under § 160.50(5)(b)(i) the chief administrator of the courts notifies the Division of Criminal Justice Services and the heads of all appropriate police departments, district attorneys' offices and other law enforcement agencies, who mark the records as expunged. Destruction is a second and distinct stage and is not automatic: § 160.50(5)(b)(i) provides that upon the written request of the individual whose case has been expunged, or their designated agent, such records shall be destroyed, and the Unified Court System publishes an application for that request through the Office of Court Administration's statewide forms library. That application is submitted to the court in which the person was convicted, one application per court of conviction; the Office of Court Administration publishes the form and does not receive it. Section 160.50(5)(b)(ii) describes what the subdivision requires as automatic vacatur, dismissal and expungement including record destruction if requested, which places the participant's request inside the same statutory mechanism rather than beside it. This is the only true erasure in New York; every other track seals. Expunged marijuana convictions do not count toward the two-conviction limit on the discretionary sealing petition, which can move a participant from ineligible to eligible there. The Marihuana Regulation and Taxation Act chapter-law citation is still not pinned and the review cites the Act generically rather than to a section.
exclusions: Any marijuana offence outside the two covered categories, being unlawful possession of marijuana and fifth-degree criminal possession of marijuana.
Mixed cases with non-marijuana charges.
Federal and out-of-state records.

waitingPeriods.duration: none. The vacatur, dismissal and expungement are automatic
none, but it is not automatic: it happens only on the participant's written request under CPL § 160.50(5)(b)(i)

units.label: The automatic vacatur, dismissal and expungement, and how to check it
units.description: The default stage, and the one that runs first. Under CPL § 160.50(5)(a) a conviction for an offence described in § 160.50(3)(k) is vacated and dismissed and all records of it expunged, by operation of law. Nothing is filed, no motion is made, no fee is charged and the participant does nothing to obtain it: under § 160.50(5)(b)(i) the chief administrator of the courts notifies the Division of Criminal Justice Services and the heads of all appropriate police departments, district attorneys' offices and other law enforcement agencies, and those holders mark the record as expunged. No participant filing exists at this stage and none is generated. The guidance explains what expungement means, that the courts do not send a notice when it happens, how to check through a DCJS Record Review, why an absence in that report is consistent with expungement rather than proof of destruction, and the separate § 160.50(5)(b)(ii)(B) route where court records cannot be located or the expungement has not been reflected. Where the participant wants nothing beyond expungement, the route ends here.

units.label: Participant-signed request to the court of conviction that the expunged records be destroyed
units.description: The conditional stage, reached only where the participant asks for destruction. It is not a chase of a failed automatic process and does not assert that anything went wrong: destruction is simply never automatic. CPL § 160.50(5)(b)(i) provides that upon the written request of the individual whose case has been expunged, or their designated agent, such records shall be destroyed, and § 160.50(5)(b)(ii) describes what the subdivision requires as automatic vacatur, dismissal and expungement including record destruction if requested. The request is therefore a conditional unit of the same statutory mechanism rather than a second remedy, and its precondition is that the case has already been expunged. The instrument is the Unified Court System's APPLICATION TO DESTROY EXPUNGED MARIHUANA CONVICTION RECORD, retained in Edition 1.2 at MRTA-DESTRUCTION-REQUEST, which the participant signs, dates and submits to the New York court in which they were convicted — a separate application to each court where they have eligible convictions — through that court's Electronic Document Delivery System, by first-class mail or in person, with no fee. This unit is a filing to a court, unlike unit 1, which has no participant document at all. What follows the submission is the court's work and not the participant's: the court acknowledges the application and forwards it to the prosecutor, the law enforcement agencies and DCJS. LegalEase prepares the participant's portion from their own answers; it does not certify eligibility, does not certify that the expungement occurred, does not advise whether to ask for destruction, does not submit the application, and does not produce a version signed by anyone but the defendant. destination.detail: Two stages with two different answers. The vacatur, dismissal and expungement happen by operation of law under CPL § 160.50(5)(a): nothing is filed, nothing is generated and the participant does nothing, while under § 160.50(5)(b)(i) the chief administrator of the courts notifies the Division of Criminal Justice Services and the police, district attorney and other law enforcement agencies that hold the records. The destruction request is a participant submission to a court. The form directs "Submit your application to the Court where you were convicted", and the instructions page adds that an application sent to a different court cannot be processed and that a person with eligible convictions in more than one court must submit a separate application to each. The Office of Court Administration publishes the form; it does not receive it, and there is no statewide OCA address, mailbox or portal for this application. What happens after submission belongs to the court: it returns an Acknowledgement of Application to Destroy Expunged Marihuana Conviction Record and forwards the application to the prosecutor, the law enforcement agencies involved and, where the person was fingerprinted, DCJS, which then writes to confirm destruction. Those are the court's acts and none of them is the participant's to perform.

Stop: the issuer's instructions require a separate application to each court of conviction, and an application sent to the wrong court cannot be processed. Next step: prepare one application per court, each signed and dated.

Destruction is irreversible and is not the same as expungement. An expunged conviction is already excluded from a Division of Criminal Justice Services criminal history report, and the statute itself contemplates that a person whose court records have been destroyed may later need to present a fingerprint record or a disposition record to have the relief assured. Say that plainly before the participant signs. LegalEase prepares the request the participant asks for; it does not advise whether to ask for destruction.

After the participant signs and submits the destruction request to the court of conviction, the court and the record holders act. The court acknowledges the application and forwards it to the prosecutor, the law enforcement agencies involved and, where the person was fingerprinted, the Division of Criminal Justice Services, which writes to confirm destruction; and under CPL § 160.50(5)(b)(i) the chief administrator of the courts is the body that notifies the record holders of the underlying expungement. The participant notifies no agency, serves nobody and delivers no certified copies, and LegalEase does not submit the application.

tracks.legalName: Clean Slate Automatic Sealing of a Driving While Ability Impaired Conviction under VTL § 1192(1) (CPL § 160.57(1)(a))
tracks.publicName: New York DWAI records and Clean Slate
tracks.mechanism: CPL § 160.57(1)(a), read at the New York State Senate's published-statutes channel on 2026-08-06, provides that convictions for subdivision one of Vehicle and Traffic Law § 1192 shall be sealed after three years. This is a traffic infraction rather than a crime; it sits in its own paragraph with its own three-year period, and the paragraph does not on its face carry the paragraph (b) conditions on pending charges, supervision status, sex offences and class A felonies. Whether those conditions nonetheless apply, and what event starts the three years, are the central open questions on this track. Nothing is filed. New York seals; it does not expunge, except for the marijuana destruction remedy. Sealed records remain accessible to law enforcement, prosecutors and courts in a new criminal case; to entities running fingerprint-based checks for work with children, the elderly and people with disabilities; to entities mandated by law to consider them; to the New York State Education Department; to private transportation network companies; to police and peace officer employers; and for firearms licensing. Federal and immigration authorities may also reach them, and a sealed conviction still counts as a predicate for sentence enhancement. New York sealing reaches New York State records only.
exclusions: Any impaired-driving conviction other than one under VTL § 1192 subdivision one. Which subdivision the conviction was under is the entire eligibility test on this track.
Federal and out-of-state records.

tracks.legalName: Discretionary Sealing by Petition (CPL § 160.59)
tracks.publicName: Petition to seal your New York convictions
tracks.mechanism: A person with up to two convictions, of which no more than one may be a felony, may petition the court of conviction to seal them at least ten years after sentencing or release, whichever is later, with time spent incarcerated after the target conviction extending the clock by an equivalent period. Crimes arising from a single criminal transaction may be treated as one conviction, and expunged marijuana convictions do not count toward the limit. There must be no open or pending criminal charges. An eligible offence is any New York crime except sex offences under Penal Law article 130 and offences requiring sex offender registration under Correction Law article 6-C, child pornography and sexual performance offences under article 263, felony homicide offences under article 125, violent felony offences as defined in Penal Law § 70.02, class A felonies, and felony conspiracy or attempt where the target offence is itself ineligible. Note the difference from Clean Slate: all class A felonies are excluded here, including article 220 drug felonies that Clean Slate carves back in. Relief is discretionary and the court weighs rehabilitation and the interests of justice. New York seals; it does not expunge, except for the marijuana destruction remedy. Sealed records remain accessible to law enforcement, prosecutors and courts in a new criminal case; to entities running fingerprint-based checks for work with children, the elderly and people with disabilities; to entities mandated by law to consider them; to the New York State Education Department; to private transportation network companies; to police and peace officer employers; and for firearms licensing. Federal and immigration authorities may also reach them, and under CPL § 160.59(10) a sealed conviction remains a predicate for sentence enhancement in a later case. New York sealing reaches New York State records only.
exclusions: Sex offences under Penal Law article 130, and any offence requiring sex offender registration under Correction Law article 6-C.
Child pornography and sexual performance by a child offences under Penal Law article 263.
Felony homicide offences under Penal Law article 125.
Violent felony offences as defined in Penal Law § 70.02.
All class A felonies, including Penal Law article 220 drug felonies. This is the opposite of the Clean Slate list and applying the wrong list is where the routing error will happen.
Felony conspiracy or attempt where the underlying target offence is not itself eligible.
More than two convictions, or more than one felony.
Any open or pending criminal charge.
Federal and out-of-state convictions.

tracks.legalName: Sealing or Expungement After a Not Guilty Finding, Dismissal, Grand Jury No Bill or Pardon (ORC 2953.33)
tracks.publicName: Clear an Ohio case that did not end in a conviction
tracks.mechanism: Where a person is found not guilty by a jury or a court, is named in a dismissed complaint, indictment or information, has a no bill entered by a grand jury, or receives a Governor's pardon, the person may apply to seal or expunge the official records. A not-guilty finding or a dismissal may be applied for at any time after the entry is made upon the minutes of the court or the journal, whichever occurs first; a no bill requires the expiration of two years after the foreperson or deputy foreperson reported it; a pardon may be applied for after the pardon or after its conditions are met. Each of these is expressly subject to ORC 2953.61. Relief is discretionary: the court determines whether a dismissal was with or without prejudice and, if without, whether the limitations period has expired, checks for pending criminal proceedings, considers prosecutor objections and weighs the applicant's interest against legitimate governmental needs. Ohio has both sealing and expungement and they are different remedies. Sealing hides the record from most public access but the record still exists and remains visible to certain employers, licensing boards, prosecutors, judges and police. Expungement is stronger and the statute uses destroy, delete and erase language. Neither may be described as "completely gone from everywhere": on a conviction expungement under ORC 2953.32 the Bureau of Criminal Identification and Investigation keeps a limited record for law-enforcement employment qualification and disqualification while other entities receiving notice must destroy, delete and erase, and that is the single most important disclosure in Ohio record-clearing copy.
exclusions: A dismissal without prejudice where the statute of limitations has not yet expired. That record is not ready and the participant must not be told it can be cleared.
Any incident where a companion charge from the same act has a different final disposition, until all related charges can be sealed or expunged together. ORC 2953.61.
Expungement, as opposed to sealing, to the extent division (C) of ORC 2953.33 limits it. That division was not read and is recorded as an open question.

tracks.legalName: Expungement of Marijuana or Hashish Possession Offences (ORC 2953.321)
tracks.publicName: Clear an Ohio marijuana or hashish possession record
tracks.mechanism: Ohio Revised Code section 2953.321, "Expungement of marijuana or hashish possession offenses", was enacted by Senate Bill 56 of the 136th General Assembly and took effect on March 20, 2026. A person convicted of, who pleaded guilty to, or whose charge was dismissed for a qualifying marijuana possession offence under specified divisions of ORC 2925.11, or a hashish possession offence involving not more than fifteen grams, may apply to the sentencing court for expungement, provided the conviction, plea or dismissal occurred before the section's effective date. The application identifies the applicant and the offence, includes evidence that the offence falls within the section, and requests expungement. On the filing of the application and payment of the fee the court sets a hearing, notifies the prosecutor of it, and directs a probation officer to make inquiries and written reports concerning the applicant; the hearing is held not less than forty-five days and not more than ninety days after the application is filed; the prosecutor may object by filing an objection with the court prior to the date set for the hearing; and the court weighs the applicant's interest against legitimate governmental needs. Unless indigent, the applicant pays a fee of fifty dollars under ORC 2953.321(G). Ohio has both sealing and expungement and they are different remedies. Sealing hides the record from most public access but the record still exists and remains visible to certain employers, licensing boards, prosecutors, judges and police. Expungement is stronger and the statute uses destroy, delete and erase language. Neither may be described as "completely gone from everywhere": on a conviction expungement under ORC 2953.32 the Bureau of Criminal Identification and Investigation keeps a limited record for law-enforcement employment qualification and disqualification while other entities receiving notice must destroy, delete and erase, and that is the single most important disclosure in Ohio record-clearing copy.
exclusions: Any conviction, plea or dismissal occurring on or after the section's March 20, 2026 effective date. The section reaches prior dispositions only.
Hashish possession involving more than fifteen grams.
Marijuana possession outside the specified divisions of ORC 2925.11.
Any incident where a companion non-marijuana charge from the same act has a different final disposition, until all related charges can be cleared together. ORC 2953.61.

tracks.legalName: Sealing of Conviction and Bail-Forfeiture Records (ORC 2953.32)
tracks.publicName: Seal an Ohio conviction
tracks.mechanism: A person convicted of an offence, or whose misdemeanour bail was forfeited, may apply to the sentencing court to seal the record once the waiting period for that conviction has run from final discharge. Final discharge means completion of the sentence, parole, all fines and all restitution, and "sentence" does not include payment of court costs, so unpaid court costs do not delay eligibility. Senate Bill 288 removed the definition of "eligible offender" from ORC 2953.31 and with it the numeric limit on how many convictions may be sealed, so Ohio is no longer a counting-caps state for sealing. Relief is discretionary: the court checks timing and pending cases, considers rehabilitation and prosecutor and victim objections, and weighs the applicant's interest against legitimate governmental needs. Ohio has both sealing and expungement and they are different remedies. Sealing hides the record from most public access but the record still exists and remains visible to certain employers, licensing boards, prosecutors, judges and police. Expungement is stronger and the statute uses destroy, delete and erase language. Neither may be described as "completely gone from everywhere": on a conviction expungement under ORC 2953.32 the Bureau of Criminal Identification and Investigation keeps a limited record for law-enforcement employment qualification and disqualification while other entities receiving notice must destroy, delete and erase, and that is the single most important disclosure in Ohio record-clearing copy.
exclusions: Offences under the traffic and motor vehicle chapters, being Chapters 4506, 4507, 4510, 4511 and 4549, or substantially similar municipal ordinances, which puts OVI outside the scheme.
A felony offence of violence that is not a sexually oriented offence.
A sexually oriented offence committed while subject to Chapter 2950 registration.
An offence where the victim was under 13, except nonsupport under ORC 2919.21.
Theft in office under ORC 2921.41.
Any felony of the first or second degree.
Domestic violence under ORC 2919.25 as a misdemeanour of the first or second degree, or a substantially similar municipal ordinance.
A felony of the third degree where the person has too many other convictions under the statute's third-degree-felony counting rule.
Any incident where a companion charge from the same act has a different final disposition, until all related charges can be cleared together. ORC 2953.61.

provenance.sourceStatement: Ohio has both sealing and expungement and they are different remedies. Sealing hides the record from most public access but the record still exists and remains visible to certain employers, licensing boards, prosecutors, judges and police. Expungement is stronger, and for many sections the statute uses destroy, delete and erase language. The reference's rule is correct and should be kept: do not say "completely gone from everywhere," and do disclose that BCI retains a limited record for law-enforcement-employment purposes on some conviction expungements.

provenance.sourceHeading: Provisions common to the Ohio tracks, The multiple-charge trap, § 2953.61
provenance.sourceStatement: where a person was charged with two or more offenses arising from the same act and at least one charge has a different final disposition from the others, the person generally cannot seal or expunge only part of the record until all related charges can be sealed or expunged together. There is a limited exception for certain traffic convictions, but the court cannot order only a portion of those records sealed. This is Ohio's most common eligibility failure and it is why the intake must capture every charge from an incident, not just the one the participant cares about.

tracks.legalName: Expungement of Conviction Records (ORC 2953.32)
tracks.publicName: Expunge an Ohio conviction
tracks.mechanism: The same section carries a second, stronger remedy on a different clock. The felony expungement clock is not ten years from discharge: it is ten years from the date the person first becomes eligible to apply for sealing for that felony, which is itself one, three or more years after discharge, so the calculation is compound and must be encoded as such rather than as a flat ten years. Expungement destroys, deletes and erases, subject to the statutory exceptions, but for conviction expungements the Bureau of Criminal Identification and Investigation keeps a limited record for law-enforcement employment qualification and disqualification. Ohio has both sealing and expungement and they are different remedies. Sealing hides the record from most public access but the record still exists and remains visible to certain employers, licensing boards, prosecutors, judges and police. Expungement is stronger and the statute uses destroy, delete and erase language. Neither may be described as "completely gone from everywhere": on a conviction expungement under ORC 2953.32 the Bureau of Criminal Identification and Investigation keeps a limited record for law-enforcement employment qualification and disqualification while other entities receiving notice must destroy, delete and erase, and that is the single most important disclosure in Ohio record-clearing copy.
exclusions: Offences under the traffic and motor vehicle chapters, being Chapters 4506, 4507, 4510, 4511 and 4549, or substantially similar municipal ordinances, which puts OVI outside the scheme.
A felony offence of violence that is not a sexually oriented offence.
A sexually oriented offence committed while subject to Chapter 2950 registration.
An offence where the victim was under 13, except nonsupport under ORC 2919.21.
Theft in office under ORC 2921.41.
Any felony of the first or second degree.
Domestic violence under ORC 2919.25 as a misdemeanour of the first or second degree, or a substantially similar municipal ordinance.
A felony of the third degree where the person has too many other convictions under the statute's third-degree-felony counting rule.
Any incident where a companion charge from the same act has a different final disposition, until all related charges can be cleared together. ORC 2953.61.

tracks.legalName: Expungement of Convictions Under the Obsolete Concealed-Handgun Notification Law (ORC 2953.35)
tracks.publicName: Clear an Ohio conviction for a gun law that no longer exists
tracks.mechanism: ORC 2953.35 provides for expungement of convictions relating to the obsolete law that required a concealed handgun licensee to promptly notify law enforcement of their firearm during an official stop. The scope is narrow and tied to specific former versions of ORC 2923.16 and ORC 2923.12; the Franklin County Law Library states that individuals with convictions prior to September 30, 2011 may apply for expungement and shredding where the conduct would now not be a crime. The application is made in the sentencing court, which checks whether the conduct would no longer violate the relevant provision, considers prosecutor objections and weighs the applicant's interest against governmental needs. The fee is fifty dollars unless indigent. This is not a general firearm expungement. Ohio has both sealing and expungement and they are different remedies. Sealing hides the record from most public access but the record still exists and remains visible to certain employers, licensing boards, prosecutors, judges and police. Expungement is stronger and the statute uses destroy, delete and erase language. Neither may be described as "completely gone from everywhere": on a conviction expungement under ORC 2953.32 the Bureau of Criminal Identification and Investigation keeps a limited record for law-enforcement employment qualification and disqualification while other entities receiving notice must destroy, delete and erase, and that is the single most important disclosure in Ohio record-clearing copy.
exclusions: Any firearm conviction other than one under the specific former versions of ORC 2923.16 and ORC 2923.12 that the section reaches. This is not a general firearm expungement and any other firearm conviction is outside it.
Conduct that would still be a crime today.
Any incident where a companion charge from the same act has a different final disposition. ORC 2953.61.

tracks.legalName: Expungement of Convictions of Human-Trafficking Survivors (ORC 2953.36)
tracks.publicName: Clearing an Ohio conviction that came from being trafficked
tracks.mechanism: ORC 2953.36 covers people convicted of prostitution-related offences under ORC 2907.24, 2907.241 or 2907.25, and people convicted of a misdemeanour or a fourth or fifth degree felony whose participation in the offence resulted from being a victim of human trafficking. An application may be made at any time and may cover more than one offence, although the court considers each separately. The standard is a preponderance of the evidence for the prostitution-related category and clear and convincing evidence for the broader misdemeanour and fourth or fifth degree felony category. Aggravated murder, murder and rape under ORC 2903.01, 2903.02 and 2907.02 are excluded. If granted, the record cannot be used for a criminal-record check and the applicant and the court may reply that no record exists. The fee is fifty dollars unless indigent. Ohio has both sealing and expungement and they are different remedies. Sealing hides the record from most public access but the record still exists and remains visible to certain employers, licensing boards, prosecutors, judges and police. Expungement is stronger and the statute uses destroy, delete and erase language. Neither may be described as "completely gone from everywhere": on a conviction expungement under ORC 2953.32 the Bureau of Criminal Identification and Investigation keeps a limited record for law-enforcement employment qualification and disqualification while other entities receiving notice must destroy, delete and erase, and that is the single most important disclosure in Ohio record-clearing copy.
exclusions: Aggravated murder, murder and rape under ORC 2903.01, 2903.02 and 2907.02, for the conviction route.
Any matter where the trafficking connection cannot be established to the applicable standard.
Any incident where a companion charge from the same act has a different final disposition. ORC 2953.61.

tracks.legalName: Expungement of Non-Conviction Records of Human-Trafficking Survivors (ORC 2953.521)
tracks.publicName: Clearing an Ohio case that came from being trafficked and did not end in conviction
tracks.mechanism: ORC 2953.521 covers a person found not guilty, or named in a dismissed complaint, indictment or information, where the case resulted from the person being a victim of human trafficking. The application may be made at any time after the not-guilty finding or dismissal is entered. The standard is a preponderance of the evidence on the trafficking connection, and the court also checks whether a dismissal was with or without prejudice and whether the limitations period has expired, checks for pending proceedings, considers prosecutor objections and weighs the governmental interest. Ohio has both sealing and expungement and they are different remedies. Sealing hides the record from most public access but the record still exists and remains visible to certain employers, licensing boards, prosecutors, judges and police. Expungement is stronger and the statute uses destroy, delete and erase language. Neither may be described as "completely gone from everywhere": on a conviction expungement under ORC 2953.32 the Bureau of Criminal Identification and Investigation keeps a limited record for law-enforcement employment qualification and disqualification while other entities receiving notice must destroy, delete and erase, and that is the single most important disclosure in Ohio record-clearing copy.
exclusions: Aggravated murder, murder and rape under ORC 2903.01, 2903.02 and 2907.02, for the conviction route.
Any matter where the trafficking connection cannot be established to the applicable standard.
Any incident where a companion charge from the same act has a different final disposition. ORC 2953.61.

tracks.legalName: Prosecutor-Initiated Sealing or Expungement of a Low-Level Controlled Substance Offence (ORC 2953.39)
tracks.publicName: When an Ohio prosecutor can clear a low-level drug record for you
tracks.mechanism: For a low-level controlled substance offence the prosecutor, not the person, may apply to the sentencing court to seal or expunge the record. A low-level controlled substance offence means certain Chapter 2925 violations that are misdemeanours of the fourth degree or minor misdemeanours, or substantially equivalent municipal ordinances. The prosecutor may file after the corresponding ORC 2953.32 waiting period expires, and the subject person and any victim may object. This is not a participant-filed route. Ohio has both sealing and expungement and they are different remedies. Sealing hides the record from most public access but the record still exists and remains visible to certain employers, licensing boards, prosecutors, judges and police. Expungement is stronger and the statute uses destroy, delete and erase language. Neither may be described as "completely gone from everywhere": on a conviction expungement under ORC 2953.32 the Bureau of Criminal Identification and Investigation keeps a limited record for law-enforcement employment qualification and disqualification while other entities receiving notice must destroy, delete and erase, and that is the single most important disclosure in Ohio record-clearing copy.
exclusions: Everything outside a Chapter 2925 violation that is a misdemeanour of the fourth degree or a minor misdemeanour, or a substantially equivalent municipal ordinance.
Any application by the person themselves. Only the prosecutor may initiate this route.

tracks.legalName: Petition to Expunge a Non-Conviction or Innocence Record (22 O.S. §§ 18 and 19)
tracks.publicName: Clear an Oklahoma arrest that did not end in a conviction
tracks.mechanism: The section 18 categories include records where the person was not charged, was acquitted, was factually innocent, or where the charge was dismissed. The petition goes to the district court in the county where the arrest information is located, the court gives thirty days' notice to the prosecuting agency, the arresting agency, the Oklahoma State Bureau of Investigation and any other agency holding relevant records, and the standard is a balancing test: the court may seal if the harm to privacy or the danger of unwarranted adverse consequences outweighs the public interest in retaining the records. Oklahoma says expungement but in most adult contexts means sealing: expungement is statutorily defined as the sealing of criminal records and of any public civil record involving actions brought by and against the State arising from the same arrest, transaction or occurrence. Fully sealed records are unavailable to the public and to law enforcement, with the Oklahoma State Bureau of Investigation retaining them for research and statistical purposes; partially sealed records are hidden from the public but remain available to law enforcement, and which category a participant lands in is a material outcome difference that must be disclosed. On an order the official actions are deemed never to have occurred, the person and criminal justice agencies may reply that no such action occurred and no such record exists, and employers, schools and state and local agencies may not require disclosure of sealed information. Title 22 section 19 does not authorise physical destruction; a sealed record may be unsealed later on a finding of changed conditions or compelling reason, and under section 19(N) a record ordered sealed that is not unsealed within ten years may be obliterated or destroyed at the end of that period.
exclusions: Not fully determined. The section 18 categories were amended by SB 2030 in 2026, by Chapter 292 O.S.L. 2025 and by Chapter 259 O.S.L. 2024, and the amended text was not read.
Federal, tribal, military and out-of-state records, which an Oklahoma order does not reach.

tracks.legalName: Petition to Expunge After a Deferred or Delayed Sentence Dismissal (22 O.S. §§ 18 and 19)
tracks.publicName: Clear an Oklahoma case after a deferred sentence was dismissed
tracks.mechanism: Where a deferred or delayed sentence has been completed and the case dismissed, the section 18 categories provide a petition route. This is distinct from the section 991c motion, which updates the court record to show the case as dismissed but does not remove the arrest record, and the two must be screened together. Oklahoma says expungement but in most adult contexts means sealing: expungement is statutorily defined as the sealing of criminal records and of any public civil record involving actions brought by and against the State arising from the same arrest, transaction or occurrence. Fully sealed records are unavailable to the public and to law enforcement, with the Oklahoma State Bureau of Investigation retaining them for research and statistical purposes; partially sealed records are hidden from the public but remain available to law enforcement, and which category a participant lands in is a material outcome difference that must be disclosed. On an order the official actions are deemed never to have occurred, the person and criminal justice agencies may reply that no such action occurred and no such record exists, and employers, schools and state and local agencies may not require disclosure of sealed information. Title 22 section 19 does not authorise physical destruction; a sealed record may be unsealed later on a finding of changed conditions or compelling reason, and under section 19(N) a record ordered sealed that is not unsealed within ten years may be obliterated or destroyed at the end of that period.
exclusions: Not fully determined. The section 18 categories were amended by SB 2030 in 2026, by Chapter 292 O.S.L. 2025 and by Chapter 259 O.S.L. 2024, and the amended text was not read.
Federal, tribal, military and out-of-state records, which an Oklahoma order does not reach.
Any record SB 2030 removed from eligibility, which is recorded as an open question.

tracks.legalName: Petition to Expunge a Misdemeanor Conviction (22 O.S. §§ 18 and 19)
tracks.publicName: Clear an Oklahoma misdemeanor conviction
tracks.mechanism: The section 18 categories provide petition routes for misdemeanour convictions on stated waiting periods and prior-record conditions. Because section 18 has been amended in three consecutive years and renumbered, the screen runs on the category description rather than the paragraph number, which is the review's single best judgment call and is preserved here. Oklahoma says expungement but in most adult contexts means sealing: expungement is statutorily defined as the sealing of criminal records and of any public civil record involving actions brought by and against the State arising from the same arrest, transaction or occurrence. Fully sealed records are unavailable to the public and to law enforcement, with the Oklahoma State Bureau of Investigation retaining them for research and statistical purposes; partially sealed records are hidden from the public but remain available to law enforcement, and which category a participant lands in is a material outcome difference that must be disclosed. On an order the official actions are deemed never to have occurred, the person and criminal justice agencies may reply that no such action occurred and no such record exists, and employers, schools and state and local agencies may not require disclosure of sealed information. Title 22 section 19 does not authorise physical destruction; a sealed record may be unsealed later on a finding of changed conditions or compelling reason, and under section 19(N) a record ordered sealed that is not unsealed within ten years may be obliterated or destroyed at the end of that period.
exclusions: Not fully determined. The section 18 categories were amended by SB 2030 in 2026, by Chapter 292 O.S.L. 2025 and by Chapter 259 O.S.L. 2024, and the amended text was not read.
Federal, tribal, military and out-of-state records, which an Oklahoma order does not reach.
Any record SB 2030 removed from eligibility, which is recorded as an open question.

tracks.legalName: Petition to Expunge After a Pardon (22 O.S. §§ 18 and 19)
tracks.publicName: Clear an Oklahoma record after a pardon
tracks.mechanism: A section 18 category provides a petition route following a pardon. Obtaining the pardon itself is a matter for the Governor and the Pardon and Parole Board and is outside scope; this track begins once the participant holds one. Oklahoma says expungement but in most adult contexts means sealing: expungement is statutorily defined as the sealing of criminal records and of any public civil record involving actions brought by and against the State arising from the same arrest, transaction or occurrence. Fully sealed records are unavailable to the public and to law enforcement, with the Oklahoma State Bureau of Investigation retaining them for research and statistical purposes; partially sealed records are hidden from the public but remain available to law enforcement, and which category a participant lands in is a material outcome difference that must be disclosed. On an order the official actions are deemed never to have occurred, the person and criminal justice agencies may reply that no such action occurred and no such record exists, and employers, schools and state and local agencies may not require disclosure of sealed information. Title 22 section 19 does not authorise physical destruction; a sealed record may be unsealed later on a finding of changed conditions or compelling reason, and under section 19(N) a record ordered sealed that is not unsealed within ten years may be obliterated or destroyed at the end of that period.
exclusions: Not fully determined. The section 18 categories were amended by SB 2030 in 2026, by Chapter 292 O.S.L. 2025 and by Chapter 259 O.S.L. 2024, and the amended text was not read.
Federal, tribal, military and out-of-state records, which an Oklahoma order does not reach.
Any record SB 2030 removed from eligibility, which is recorded as an open question.

tracks.legalName: Petition to Expunge an Identity Theft or Wrong-Person Record (22 O.S. § 18 identity-theft category, with § 19a)
tracks.publicName: Clear an Oklahoma record that is not yours
tracks.mechanism: Where a record was created in the participant's name through identity theft, or otherwise identifies the wrong person, the section 18 identity-theft category with section 19a provides the route. The review classifies this as custom_pleading and approves it with limitations. Oklahoma says expungement but in most adult contexts means sealing: expungement is statutorily defined as the sealing of criminal records and of any public civil record involving actions brought by and against the State arising from the same arrest, transaction or occurrence. Fully sealed records are unavailable to the public and to law enforcement, with the Oklahoma State Bureau of Investigation retaining them for research and statistical purposes; partially sealed records are hidden from the public but remain available to law enforcement, and which category a participant lands in is a material outcome difference that must be disclosed. On an order the official actions are deemed never to have occurred, the person and criminal justice agencies may reply that no such action occurred and no such record exists, and employers, schools and state and local agencies may not require disclosure of sealed information. Title 22 section 19 does not authorise physical destruction; a sealed record may be unsealed later on a finding of changed conditions or compelling reason, and under section 19(N) a record ordered sealed that is not unsealed within ten years may be obliterated or destroyed at the end of that period.
exclusions: Not fully determined. The section 18 categories were amended by SB 2030 in 2026, by Chapter 292 O.S.L. 2025 and by Chapter 259 O.S.L. 2024, and the amended text was not read.

Title 22 section 19 does not authorise physical destruction; a sealed record may be unsealed later on a finding of changed conditions or compelling reason, and under section 19(N) a record ordered sealed that is not unsealed within ten years may be obliterated or destroyed at the end of that period.

tracks.legalName: Motion to Expunge the Court Record of a Completed Deferred Sentence (22 O.S. § 991c)
tracks.publicName: Update an Oklahoma deferred sentence so the case shows as dismissed
tracks.mechanism: A section 991c expungement updates the court record of a completed deferred sentence so the case shows as dismissed. It is not a full record clearing: the Oklahoma State Bureau of Investigation states in terms that "A Section 991(c) expungement will not expunge (remove) the arrest record." The review calls this the most important consumer-facing point in Oklahoma, because a participant who obtains only a section 991c order and is told their record is clear has been misled. Every section 991c motion is therefore paired with a section 18 arrest-record screen. Oklahoma says expungement but in most adult contexts means sealing. Fully sealed records are unavailable to the public and to law enforcement, with OSBI retaining them for research and statistical purposes; partially sealed records are hidden from the public but remain available to law enforcement. Title 22 section 19 does not authorise physical destruction, a sealed record may be unsealed on changed conditions or a compelling reason, and under section 19(N) a sealed record not unsealed within ten years may be obliterated or destroyed.
exclusions: The arrest record, which a section 991c order does not reach. That needs a section 18 petition and carries the $150 OSBI processing fee.
Any deferred sentence that has not been completed.

tracks.legalName: Clean Slate Sealing Without Petition (22 O.S. §§ 18b and 19d, as enacted by Senate Bill 2030, Laws 2026, c. 282)
tracks.publicName: Oklahoma's automatic record sealing, and where it stands
tracks.mechanism: Senate Bill 2030 was enacted and is in force. It was approved by the Governor on 11 May 2026 after the emergency was adopted in both chambers, it is codified as Laws 2026, c. 282, and the codifier records the amendment as effective 1 July 2026. The Act amends 22 O.S. §§ 18 and 19, creates 22 O.S. §§ 18b and 19d, and repeals a duplicate § 18. Sections 19a, 60.18 and 991c are untouched. The former § 18(C) route — automatic sealing of clean slate eligible ARREST records, on a trigger that had already passed — was repealed, and the § 19(B) machinery that ran it was removed. Eligibility now sits in § 18b and the process in § 19d. Section 18b(B) provides that "Beginning on the effective date of this act and subject to the availability of funds, individuals with clean slate eligible records shall be eligible to have their records sealed without filing a court petition." So statutory eligibility exists today; administration does not. Section 19d(A) requires the Oklahoma State Bureau of Investigation to establish a publicly accessible online portal for expedited expungement requests by 1 November 2026. Section 19d(D) requires the Bureau to begin implementing the automatic process on or before 1 November 2027, and requires all electronic records eligible through that process on or after 1 November 2027 to be identified and expunged before 1 November 2029. The Act widened the eligible set rather than narrowing it. Section 18b reaches records rather than arrest records only, expressly including court records, sets a temporal floor of 1 January 1980, carries forward the new § 18(A)(15) identity-theft category, and adds two conviction categories the repealed route never reached at all: a 63 O.S. § 2-402(A)(1) felony where the person is not currently serving a sentence, five years have passed since the end of the last felony or misdemeanour sentence and the record is single-source; and a misdemeanour conviction with no felony conviction, no pending charges, five years since the end of the last misdemeanour sentence and a single-source record. What it removed was the earlier, narrower route, not a participant's category. Neither the automatic process nor the portal is operating. The Bureau's own criminal history record expungement page, last updated 23 July 2026 and therefore after the Act took effect, describes no portal and does not state that automatic sealing is operating. Both statutory deadlines are in the future. The right to petition is expressly preserved. Section 19d(G) reads "Nothing in this section precludes an individual from filing a petition with the district court pursuant to Section 19 of Title 22 of the Oklahoma Statutes for expungement of clean slate eligible records", and § 19(A) is undisturbed. The petition routes are the only routes an Oklahoma participant can use today. Records sealed through the clean slate route are PARTIALLY sealed under § 18b(D): unavailable to the public, still available to law enforcement for law enforcement purposes, and still admissible under § 18b(E) to prove a prior conviction or deferred judgment without an unsealing order. Oklahoma says expungement but in most adult contexts means sealing. Title 22 § 19 does not authorise physical destruction, a sealed record may be unsealed on changed conditions or a compelling reason, and under § 19(L) — the ten-year obliteration rule, which the pre-2026 lettering carried further down the section — a sealed record not unsealed within ten years may be obliterated or destroyed.
exclusions: Everyone, as a route to use today. Statutory eligibility exists under 22 O.S. § 18b(B), but the automatic process is not operating and the request portal is not published.

tracks.mechanism: Senate Bill 2030 was enacted and is in force. Section 19d(B) limits what the request may require to sufficient personal identification information for the Bureau to locate the record and contact information for notification. Section 19d(C) sets the review sequence: the Bureau reviews the record, solicits review by the arresting and prosecuting agencies, sends a request to the district court on confirmation, and where any party finds the record ineligible sends the individual a written or electronic notice of rejection stating the reasons. The statute sets no fee for the request. Neither the automatic process nor the portal is operating. The Bureau's own criminal history record expungement page, last updated 23 July 2026 and therefore after the Act took effect, describes no portal and does not state that automatic sealing is operating. Both statutory deadlines are in the future. The right to petition is expressly preserved. Section 19d(G) reads "Nothing in this section precludes an individual from filing a petition with the district court pursuant to Section 19 of Title 22 of the Oklahoma Statutes for expungement of clean slate eligible records", and § 19(A) is undisturbed. The petition routes are the only routes an Oklahoma participant can use today. Records sealed through the clean slate route are PARTIALLY sealed under § 18b(D): unavailable to the public, still available to law enforcement for law enforcement purposes, and still admissible under § 18b(E) to prove a prior conviction or deferred judgment without an unsealing order. Oklahoma says expungement but in most adult contexts means sealing. Title 22 § 19 does not authorise physical destruction, a sealed record may be unsealed on changed conditions or a compelling reason, and under § 19(L) — the ten-year obliteration rule, which the pre-2026 lettering carried further down the section — a sealed record not unsealed within ten years may be obliterated or destroyed.
exclusions: Everyone, as a route to use today. No portal is published and nothing can be submitted through one.
Any record outside the § 18b(A) clean slate eligible set or § 18(A)(16), which are the only records the portal reaches.

tracks.legalName: Motion to Set Aside the Record of an Arrest, Citation or Charge Where No Accusatory Instrument Was Filed (ORS 137.225(1)(c))
tracks.publicName: Set aside an Oregon arrest that never led to charges
tracks.mechanism: Where no accusatory instrument is filed, at any time after 60 days from the date the prosecuting attorney indicates that the state has elected not to proceed with a prosecution or contempt proceeding, an arrested, cited or charged person may apply to the court in the county in which the person was arrested, cited or charged for an order setting aside the record of the arrest, citation or charge. The clock runs from the prosecutor's declination, not from the arrest. Under ORS 137.225(3)(b) the court shall grant a motion under this paragraph. There is no filing fee under ORS 137.225(1)(g). Oregon calls it a set-aside and there are no separate sealing and expungement tracks: the court sets aside and seals, and under ORS 137.225(4) the conviction, arrest, citation, charge or other proceeding is deemed not to have occurred and the person may answer accordingly any questions relating to its occurrence. The order reaches Oregon court and law enforcement records including the Oregon State Police LEDS system. It does not reach federal or other states' records. Under 2024 Oregon State Police policy a set-aside does not restore firearm rights; a separate restoration process is required. Two statutory carve-outs survive: under ORS 137.225(10) the deemed-not-to-have-occurred rule does not apply in a civil action where truth is an element of a claim or defence, and a party may apply for disclosure; and under ORS 137.225(11) a court may order records reopened on a prosecutor's or defendant's motion supported by affidavit showing good cause, and a prosecuting attorney may unseal a set-aside arrest, citation or charge to initiate a proceeding within the statute of limitations, on written notice to the person.
exclusions: An arrest or citation for driving while under the influence of intoxicants where the charge is dismissed as a result of the person's successful completion of a diversion agreement described in ORS 813.200. ORS 137.225(8)(a).
The dismissal of a citation for a traffic violation. ORS 137.225(8)(b).

A person who, at the time the motion is pending before the court, is under charge of commission of any crime or of contempt of court for violating an order related to abuse or a person crime. ORS 137.225(7)(a)(C).
Federal and other states' records, which ORS 137.225 cannot reach.

tracks.legalName: Motion to Set Aside the Record After an Acquittal (ORS 137.225(1)(d))
tracks.publicName: Set aside an Oregon charge you were acquitted of
tracks.mechanism: At any time after an acquittal, an arrested, cited or charged person may apply to the court in the county in which the person was arrested, cited or charged for an order setting aside the record of the arrest, citation or charge. There is no waiting period and, under ORS 137.225(9), no time limit for making an application. Under ORS 137.225(3)(b) the court shall grant a motion under this paragraph. Oregon calls it a set-aside and there are no separate sealing and expungement tracks: the court sets aside and seals, and under ORS 137.225(4) the conviction, arrest, citation, charge or other proceeding is deemed not to have occurred and the person may answer accordingly any questions relating to its occurrence. The order reaches Oregon court and law enforcement records including the Oregon State Police LEDS system. It does not reach federal or other states' records. Under 2024 Oregon State Police policy a set-aside does not restore firearm rights; a separate restoration process is required. Two statutory carve-outs survive: under ORS 137.225(10) the deemed-not-to-have-occurred rule does not apply in a civil action where truth is an element of a claim or defence, and a party may apply for disclosure; and under ORS 137.225(11) a court may order records reopened on a prosecutor's or defendant's motion supported by affidavit showing good cause, and a prosecuting attorney may unseal a set-aside arrest, citation or charge to initiate a proceeding within the statute of limitations, on written notice to the person.
exclusions: An arrest or citation for driving while under the influence of intoxicants where the charge is dismissed as a result of the person's successful completion of a diversion agreement described in ORS 813.200. ORS 137.225(8)(a).
The dismissal of a citation for a traffic violation. ORS 137.225(8)(b).

A person who, at the time the motion is pending before the court, is under charge of commission of any crime or of contempt of court for violating an order related to abuse or a person crime. ORS 137.225(7)(a)(C).
Federal and other states' records.

tracks.legalName: Motion to Set Aside a Conviction (ORS 137.225(1)(a) and (1)(b))
tracks.publicName: Set aside an Oregon conviction
tracks.mechanism: A person convicted of an offence who has fully complied with and performed the sentence of the court, and whose conviction is described in ORS 137.225(5), may move the court where the conviction was entered for an order setting it aside once eligible under ORS 137.225(1)(b). A person still under supervision as part of that sentence has not fully complied. The tiers run seven years for a Class B felony, five years for a Class C felony, three years for a Class A misdemeanor and one year for a Class B or C misdemeanor or a violation, each measured from the date of conviction or the release from imprisonment for the conviction sought to be set aside, whichever is later. Where the court has reduced the offence classification the applicable period is the one associated with the reduced classification. Where probation was revoked, no application may be made for three years from the revocation or until the person becomes eligible under the ordinary tier, whichever is later. There is no filing fee. Oregon calls it a set-aside and there are no separate sealing and expungement tracks: the court sets aside and seals, and under ORS 137.225(4) the conviction, arrest, citation, charge or other proceeding is deemed not to have occurred and the person may answer accordingly any questions relating to its occurrence. The order reaches Oregon court and law enforcement records including the Oregon State Police LEDS system. It does not reach federal or other states' records. Under 2024 Oregon State Police policy a set-aside does not restore firearm rights; a separate restoration process is required. Two statutory carve-outs survive: under ORS 137.225(10) the deemed-not-to-have-occurred rule does not apply in a civil action where truth is an element of a claim or defence, and a party may apply for disclosure; and under ORS 137.225(11) a court may order records reopened on a prosecutor's or defendant's motion supported by affidavit showing good cause, and a prosecuting attorney may unseal a set-aside arrest, citation or charge to initiate a proceeding within the statute of limitations, on written notice to the person.
exclusions: A conviction for a state or municipal traffic offence. ORS 137.225(7)(a)(A).
A Class B felony that is a violation of ORS 166.429, or any crime classified as a person felony under the rules of the Oregon Criminal Justice Commission. ORS 137.225(5)(a).

Criminal mistreatment in the second degree under ORS 163.200 where the victim was 65 or older; criminal mistreatment in the first degree under ORS 163.205 where the victim was 65 or older or the offence constitutes child abuse; endangering the welfare of a minor under ORS 163.575(1)(a) where the offence constitutes child abuse; criminally negligent homicide under ORS 163.145 punishable as a Class C felony; and assault in the third degree under ORS 163.165(1)(h). ORS 137.225(6)(a) to (e).

Any sex crime, subject to the narrow carve-backs in ORS 137.225(6)(f) for offences listed in ORS 163A.140(1)(a) where the reporting obligation has been relieved, and for certain Class C felony sex crimes meeting the age, age-difference, consent-incapacity and same-victim conditions.

A conviction of any other offence within the applicable look-back period, excluding motor vehicle violations, a single non-motor-vehicle violation and unlawful possession of a controlled substance constituting a drug enforcement misdemeanour. ORS 137.225(7)(a)(B) and (7)(b).
A person under charge of any crime, or of contempt of court for violating an order related to abuse or a person crime, at the time the motion is pending. ORS 137.225(7)(a)(C).
Federal and other states' convictions, which ORS 137.225 cannot reach.

releaseBlockers.question: Whether a conviction arising from the same criminal episode as the offence being set aside counts as a disqualifying other conviction. The controlling review states that it does not, calls the same-episode rule the clearest treatment of any single doctrine in the series and directs that it be preserved in the engine. The enacted text of Oregon Laws 2025 chapter 349, read at the Oregon Legislature's own channel on 2026-08-06, reads the other way on its face: ORS 137.225(7)(a)(B) disqualifies a person convicted of any other offence within the applicable period "whether or not the other conviction is for conduct associated with the same criminal episode". The enacted text does carve out motor vehicle violations, unlawful possession of a controlled substance constituting a drug enforcement misdemeanour, and under ORS 137.225(7)(b) a single non-motor-vehicle violation; the Oregon Judicial Department's own packet describes the carve-out the same way, as "except traffic violations or a single violation offense", and does not mention same-episode convictions. Neither reading is adopted here and no eligibility statement is made where a second conviction from the same episode is in play.

provenance.sourceStatement: A person convicted ... of any other offense, excluding motor vehicle violations and unlawful possession of a controlled substance constituting a drug enforcement misdemeanor ..., or found in contempt of court for violating an order related to abuse or a person crime, within the following applicable time period immediately preceding the filing of the motion pursuant to subsection (1)(a) of this section, whether or not the other conviction is for conduct associated with the same criminal episode that caused the conviction, or with the same course of conduct that caused the finding, that is sought to be set aside

releaseBlockers.question: The current Oregon State Police record-check fee. ORS 137.225(2)(d) as enacted leaves the figure to the department, capped at actual cost, so the review's reported figure of about $33 per conviction cannot be confirmed from the statute and the department's current schedule was not obtained. The statute does settle one thing the review did not have: where the department performs only one record check it may charge only one fee regardless of how many counties the person files in.

provenance.sourceStatement: The department shall establish a fee in an amount not to exceed the actual cost of performing the criminal record check. If the department is required to perform only one criminal record check for the person, the department may only charge one fee, regardless of the number of counties in which the person is filing a motion to set aside a conviction, finding, arrest, charge or citation under this section.

releaseBlockers.question: How far the 2025 monetary-obligations relief actually reaches. The controlling review describes Oregon Laws 2025 chapter 395 section 1 as a general rule that expired judgment remedies for monetary obligations in any judgment of conviction count as sentence completion. The enacted text read at the Oregon Legislature's own channel on 2026-08-06 is narrower in its operative first subsection: it expires the judgment remedies for a judgment entered in a municipal court or justice court for a pre-July 1, 2015 marijuana-possession offence under one ounce. Subsection (2) then applies the sentence-completion consequence to obligations that have expired "under subsection (1) of this section". Whether the consequence in subsection (2) reaches obligations that expire under ORS 18.194 generally, or only those expired by subsection (1), is the difference between a broad unlock and a marijuana-specific one.

provenance.sourceStatement: (1) Notwithstanding ORS 18.194, judgment remedies for a judgment of conviction entered in a municipal court or justice court for violating, prior to July 1, 2015, a city or county ordinance or state statute prohibiting the possession of less than one ounce of marijuana, that have not yet expired under the provisions of ORS 18.194, expire on the effective date of this 2025 Act. (2) If the judgment remedies for monetary obligations in a judgment of conviction have expired under subsection (1) of this section, a person shall be considered to have completed, fully complied with and performed the sentence of the court with respect to those monetary obligations for purposes of ORS 137.225 or 475C.397 or any other statute authorizing the court to set aside the judgment of conviction.

releaseBlockers.question: Whether the categorical exclusion lists in ORS 137.225(5), (6) and (7)(a)(A) as enacted have been amended again since Oregon Laws 2025 chapter 349, and how the person-felony and person Class A misdemeanor definitions in the rules of the Oregon Criminal Justice Commission map to particular offences. The exclusion screen depends on a classification the participant cannot supply.
