tracks.legalName: Solicitor Application to Expunge a First Low-Level Conviction or a Domestic Violence Third-Degree Conviction, S.C. Code § 22-5-910
tracks.publicName: Clear a low-level South Carolina conviction after three years
tracks.mechanism: Read at source on 2026-08-06, § 22-5-910(A) allows a defendant convicted of a crime carrying a penalty of not more than thirty days imprisonment or a one thousand dollar fine, or both, or a first offence for unlawful possession of a firearm or weapon carrying not more than one year or a one thousand dollar fine, or both, to apply after three years from the date of the conviction to the circuit court for an order expunging the records of the arrest and conviction and any associated bench warrant; the section does not apply to an offence involving the operation of a motor vehicle. Subsection (B) sets five years for a domestic violence third degree conviction under § 16-25-20(D), or § 16-25-20(B)(1) as it existed before June 4, 2015. Subsection (C) requires no other conviction, including out-of-state convictions, during the applicable period. Subsection (E) defines conviction to include a guilty plea, a plea of nolo contendere or the forfeiting of bail, and provides that any number of subsection (A) offences sentenced at a single sentencing proceeding that are closely connected and arose out of the same incident may be treated as one conviction for expungement purposes. Subsection (F) bars expungement where the person has pending criminal charges of any kind unless they have been pending more than five years, tolled for any time under a bench warrant for failure to appear, allows the relief once only, and applies retroactively. Section 17-22-940(D) requires the summary court judge to attest, and § 17-22-940(E) requires SLED verification with the $25 fee.
exclusions: Any offence involving the operation of a motor vehicle, § 22-5-910(A).

Any conviction carrying a penalty greater than thirty days imprisonment or a one thousand dollar fine, other than a first offence of unlawful possession of a firearm or weapon carrying not more than one year or a one thousand dollar fine.
Any person with another conviction, including an out-of-state conviction, during the three-year or five-year period.
Any person with criminal charges pending of any kind, unless they have been pending more than five years, and that period is tolled for any time under a bench warrant for failure to appear.
Any person who has already used the section once.
The SLED nonpublic record retained under § 22-5-910(D).

tracks.legalName: Solicitor Application to Expunge a First-Offence Youthful Offender Act Conviction, S.C. Code § 22-5-920
tracks.publicName: Clear a South Carolina conviction you were sentenced for under the Youthful Offender Act
tracks.mechanism: Read at source on 2026-08-06, § 22-5-920(B)(1) allows a defendant with a first offence conviction as a youthful offender, for which the defendant was sentenced pursuant to Chapter 19 of Title 24, the Youthful Offender Act, and who has not been convicted of any offence including an out-of-state offence while serving the youthful offender sentence including probation and parole and for a period of five years from the date of completion of that sentence, to apply to the circuit court for an order expunging the records of the arrest and conviction. Convictions for driving under suspension, and for disturbing schools under § 16-17-420 before May 17, 2018, are excepted from the disqualifying set. Subsection (B)(2) excludes an offence involving the operation of a motor vehicle, an offence classified as a violent crime in § 16-1-60, an offence contained in Chapter 25 of Title 16 except as otherwise provided in § 16-25-30, and an offence for which registration is required under the Sex Offender Registry Act. Subsection (B)(3) makes the relief once only and applies it retroactively. Subsection (A) defines conviction to include a guilty plea, a plea of nolo contendere or the forfeiting of bail, and allows any number of offences receiving a youthful offender sentence at a single sentencing proceeding that are closely connected and arose out of the same incident to be treated as one conviction for expungement purposes. Section 17-22-940(E) requires SLED verification with the $25 fee and provides that a minor traffic-related conviction unrelated to driving under the influence is not a bar.
exclusions: Any person who was merely eligible for a Youthful Offender Act sentence but was not actually sentenced under Chapter 19 of Title 24.
Any offence involving the operation of a motor vehicle, § 22-5-920(B)(2)(a).
Any offence classified as a violent crime in § 16-1-60, § 22-5-920(B)(2)(b).
Any offence contained in Chapter 25 of Title 16, except as otherwise provided in § 16-25-30, § 22-5-920(B)(2)(c).
Any offence for which registration is required under the South Carolina Sex Offender Registry Act, § 22-5-920(B)(2)(d).

Any person convicted of any offence, including an out-of-state offence, while serving the youthful offender sentence or during the five years following its completion, other than a conviction for driving under suspension or for disturbing schools under § 16-17-420 before May 17, 2018.
Any person who has already used the section once.

releaseBlockers.question: The single-incident fee. Section 17-22-940(G) as amended by 2018 Act No. 254 was read at source on 2026-08-06 and provides that where multiple charges from a single incident are combined under § 17-1-40 or § 17-22-150(a), 'only one two hundred fifty-dollar fee, one twenty-five dollar SLED verification fee, and one thirty-five dollar clerk of court filing fee may be charged'. The controlling review reports the single-incident solicitor fee as one hundred fifty dollars, drawn from Supreme Court expungement guidance. The current statutory figure is two hundred fifty dollars. The packet quotes the statutory figure and does not promise the lower one.

provenance.sourceStatement: There is a second, lower solicitor fee the reference does not mention. The standard administrative fee is $250, but the Supreme Court's expungement guidance provides that where expungement is sought for **multiple charges arising out of a single incident** under §§ 17-1-40 or 17-22-150(a), those charges may go on **one application** and only **one fee of $150** is charged, plus one $25 SLED verification fee and one $35 clerk fee where applicable.
provenance.counselQuestion: Does the $150 single-incident fee in the Supreme Court guidance survive the 2018 amendment to § 17-22-940(G), which says only one $250 fee may be charged in that circumstance? Which figure does the packet quote?

tracks.legalName: Solicitor Application to Expunge a First-Offence Drug Conviction, S.C. Code § 22-5-930
tracks.publicName: Clear a first South Carolina drug conviction
tracks.mechanism: Read in full at source on 2026-08-06, § 22-5-930 has two branches. Subsection (A) reaches a first offence conviction for either simple possession of a controlled substance under Article 3 of Chapter 53, Title 44, or unlawful possession of a prescription drug under § 40-43-86(EE), including charges for which the person would now be eligible for a conditional discharge under § 44-53-450, and allows application to the circuit court three years from the date of completion of the sentence including probation and parole, whether the conviction was in magistrates or general sessions court. Subsection (B) reaches a first offence conviction for possession with intent to distribute a controlled substance under the same article and allows application twenty years from the date of completion of any sentence including probation and parole for a drug conviction or any felony conviction. Subsection (C) requires no other conviction, including out-of-state convictions, during the three-year period, or no other drug or felony conviction during the twenty-year period. Subsection (D) bars expungement while criminal charges of any kind are pending unless they have been pending more than five years, tolled for time under a bench warrant for failure to appear; allows the relief once only; and bars it where the person has had a conditional discharge within the five years before the arrest for a simple possession of marijuana charge, or within the ten years before the arrest for any other controlled substance or a prescription drug charge. The section applies retroactively but does not affect a pre-existing enhanced conviction or sentence. Subsection (E) requires SLED to keep a nonpublic record.
exclusions: Any drug conviction that is not a first offence within the meaning of the subsection relied on.

Any person with another conviction, including an out-of-state conviction, during the three-year period under subsection (A), or another drug or felony conviction during the twenty-year period under subsection (B).
Any person with criminal charges pending of any kind, unless they have been pending more than five years, tolled for time under a bench warrant for failure to appear.
Any person who has already used the section once.

Any person who had a conditional discharge within the five years before the arrest, where the charge sought to be expunged is simple possession of marijuana, or within the ten years before the arrest for any other controlled substance or an unlawful prescription drug charge.
The SLED nonpublic record retained under § 22-5-930(E).
Any drug offence outside the two branches. The review's warning against routing all drug convictions here stands.

tracks.legalName: Solicitor Application to Expunge a First-Offence Failure to Stop for a Blue Light Conviction, S.C. Code § 56-5-750(F)
tracks.publicName: Clear a first South Carolina failure-to-stop-for-a-blue-light conviction after three years
tracks.mechanism: Read at source on 2026-08-06, § 56-5-750(F) provides that after a conviction pursuant to subsection (B)(1) for a first offence, the person may, after three years from the date of completion of all terms and conditions of the sentence for the first offence, apply or cause someone acting on his behalf to apply to the court for an order expunging the records of the arrest and conviction. The provision does not apply to any crime classified as a felony. If the person has had no other conviction during the three-year period following completion of the terms and conditions, the court shall issue the order. No person has any rights under the section more than one time. After expungement both SLED and the Department of Motor Vehicles keep a nonpublic record of the offence and the date of expungement to prevent a second use, exempt from the Freedom of Information Act except to authorised officials. The review's caution about the amendment effective 12 May 2026 is answered: 2025 Act No. 38 (H.3127), section 1, effective May 12, 2026, reenacted subsection (A) unchanged, altered the subsection (B)(1) and (B)(2) penalties, added subsection (B)(3), and raised the subsection (C)(1) and (C)(2) penalties; it did not amend subsection (F), whose three-year first-offence expungement is unchanged. Section 17-22-940(E) requires SLED verification with the $25 fee and provides that a minor traffic-related conviction unrelated to driving under the influence is not a bar.
exclusions: Any conviction other than a first offence pursuant to § 56-5-750(B)(1). Convictions under subsections (B)(2), (B)(3) or (C) are outside the route.
Any crime classified as a felony, which § 56-5-750(F) expressly excludes.
Any person with another conviction during the three-year period following completion of all terms and conditions of the sentence.
Any person who has already used the section once.
The SLED and Department of Motor Vehicles nonpublic records retained under § 56-5-750(F).

waitingPeriods.duration: Three years from the date of completion of all terms and conditions of the sentence, with no other conviction during that period. The clock runs from completion of every term and condition, not from the conviction date.

$250 solicitor administrative fee per individual order under § 17-22-940(A), nonrefundable even if the charge is later found ineligible; $25 SLED verification fee under § 17-22-940(E)(1); and the $35 clerk of court filing fee under § 17-22-940(F) and § 8-21-310(C)(4), which the solicitor forwards and which is refunded if the charge is found statutorily ineligible. Under § 17-22-940(E), on this route a conviction for any minor traffic-related offence that is not related in any way to driving under the influence of alcohol or other drugs is not considered a bar to expungement.

tracks.legalName: Solicitor Application to Expunge an Old Unlawful Handgun Possession Conviction, S.C. Code § 17-1-65
tracks.publicName: Clear an old South Carolina unlawful handgun possession conviction — the window closes 7 March 2029
tracks.mechanism: Read at source on 2026-08-06, § 17-1-65 provides that a person may apply for an expungement of one conviction for unlawful possession of a handgun as provided in § 16-23-20, if the conviction occurred prior to the enactment of the South Carolina Constitutional Carry/Second Amendment Preservation Act of 2024, and that an application under the section must be made within five years of the enactment of the section. The section was created by 2024 Act No. 111 (H.3594), § 20, effective March 7, 2024, which fixes both dates: the conviction must predate March 7, 2024, and the application must be made before March 7, 2029. SCCA 223C (06/2024), read at source on the same date, is the instrument for this route and not a general-purpose General Sessions destruction order: it recites that the defendant is entitled to have the records expunged 'according to S.C. Code Ann. § 17-1-65' and carries three findings tracking the section exactly — conviction under § 16-23-20 prior to the enactment of the Act on March 7, 2024; application submitted prior to March 7, 2029; and no previous application for expungement of a handgun possession conviction under § 17-1-65. The form also recites the § 17-1-40 sealed retentions and the § 22-5-910 SLED nonpublic retention, so the surviving records are stated on the order itself. This is a closing window and the deadline should be surfaced unprompted.
exclusions: Any conviction for unlawful possession of a handgun occurring on or after March 7, 2024, the date the Constitutional Carry/Second Amendment Preservation Act of 2024 was enacted.
Any conviction under a provision other than § 16-23-20.
More than one conviction; the section reaches one conviction only.
Any person who has previously applied for expungement of a handgun possession conviction under § 17-1-65.
Any application made on or after March 7, 2029, when the five-year window closes permanently.
The sealed and nonpublic retentions the SCCA 223C order itself recites under §§ 17-1-40 and 22-5-910.

waitingPeriods.duration: None. Section 17-1-65 imposes no waiting period. It imposes a deadline instead: the application must be made within five years of the section's enactment, that is before March 7, 2029.

Open question blocks release (filing_process): The single-incident fee. Section 17-22-940(G) as amended by 2018 Act No. 254 was read at source on 2026-08-06 and provides that where multiple charges from a single incident are combined under § 17-1-40 or § 17-22-150(a), 'only one two hundred fifty-dollar fee, one twenty-five dollar SLED verification fee, and one thirty-five dollar clerk of court filing fee may be charged'. The controlling review reports the single-incident solicitor fee as one hundred fifty dollars, drawn from Supreme Court expungement guidance. The current statutory figure is two hundred fifty dollars. The packet quotes the statutory figure and does not promise the lower one.

tracks.legalName: Motion for Expungement of Arrest Record (SDCL §§ 23A-3-26 to 23A-3-32)
tracks.publicName: Expunge a South Dakota arrest record
tracks.mechanism: An arrested person may apply to the court that would have jurisdiction over the crime for which the person was arrested for an order expunging the record of the arrest: after one year from the arrest where no accusatory instrument was filed; after one year from the date the prosecuting attorney formally dismisses the entire criminal case on the record; at any time after an acquittal; or within one year of a formal dismissal of the entire case on a showing of compelling necessity. The motion starts a new civil action, may be made only on a record of arrest, and more than one arrest record requires a separate case for each. The court may enter the order only after finding by clear and convincing evidence that the ends of justice and the best interests of the public and the defendant or arrested person will be served. Expungement in South Dakota means sealing, not destruction, and a nonpublic disposition record is retained by the Division of Criminal Investigation.
exclusions: Partial dismissals. Both the statute and the review turn on the ENTIRE criminal case being formally dismissed on the record; where some counts were dismissed and others resolved otherwise, this track is unavailable.
Convictions of any kind, which this track does not reach; South Dakota is not a broad adult conviction-expungement state.
Federal, tribal, military and out-of-state records, which South Dakota relief does not reach.
More than one arrest record in a single filing; each arrest record requires its own civil action and its own fee.

units.label: Disposition classification, timing analysis and arrest-record count
units.description: The judgment stage, and the one that decides whether anything can be filed at all. Establish the correct court and county; establish whether the entire criminal case was formally dismissed on the record rather than partially; establish which of the four § 23A-3-27 timing branches applies and whether its clock has run; and count how many separate arrest records are involved, because each one requires its own civil action and its own $72 fee. The participant is directed to obtain the dismissal order, the acquittal judgment or proof that no accusatory instrument was filed, plus the court docket and a DCI criminal history. Nothing is filed at this stage and LegalEase does not receive, inspect or authenticate any of those records.

units.label: UJS motion packet: UJS-232, UJS-391 and the proposed UJS-394 order
units.description: The document stage. The South Dakota Unified Judicial System publishes a complete statewide form set, so the document work is form-fill and no custom pleading is advisable. LegalEase completes UJS-232 Case Filing Statement, UJS-391 Motion for Expungement and Statement of Mailing, and the proposed UJS-394 Order for Expungement which the judge signs. UJS-392 Waiver of Hearing is prepared conditionally, only where the arrested person, the prosecutor and any victim will all waive. UJS-393 Notice of Hearing is prepared conditionally where a hearing is required. The forms are identified by number and use but were not supplied in the archive; acquiring the current revisions is carried as a legal-design blocker on this track.

units.label: Filing, fee or indigency request, service on the State's Attorney, hearing or waiver, and UJS-395
units.description: The procedural stage, which runs after the packet exists and continues after the judge signs. File the new civil action with the clerk and pay the $72 civil filing fee or request indigency relief; mail or serve the State's Attorney, who may contest; serve any notice of hearing at least fourteen days before the hearing; coordinate the three-party waiver where all of the person, the prosecutor and any victim agree; and after the order is signed prepare and file UJS-395 Notice of Entry of Order and mail it with the order to the State's Attorney. This stage is guidance because its substance is timing, service and coordination with parties the participant does not control, not document production.

selfHelpBoundaries: Only some charges in the case were dismissed. A partial dismissal defeats this track; the statute requires the ENTIRE criminal case to have been formally dismissed on the record.
A compelling-necessity filing inside the one-year window, which is an argument rather than a fact.
Any victim who may object or whose waiver is needed.
Prosecutor opposition, or any contested hearing.
More than one arrest record, which means more than one civil action and more than one fee.
Arrests in more than one county.

Federal, tribal, military or out-of-state records. Tribal records are a live South Dakota issue given the number of reservations and concurrent-jurisdiction questions, and are an explicit escalation rather than a footnote.
Immigration exposure.
Any adult conviction that is not clearly SIS-based, pardon-based, diversion-based or minor-case automatic removal.
Any felony, DUI, domestic violence, sex offence, child-victim offence, violence, firearm or protection-order issue.

Compelling necessity and the clear-and-convincing findings are outside self-help. LegalEase must not state that the ends of justice and the best interests of the public will be served, or that compelling necessity exists.
Tribal records are their own escalation in South Dakota given the number of reservations and the frequency of concurrent-jurisdiction questions, not a line inside a general out-of-state bullet.
packetInstructions: One civil action per arrest record. More than one arrest record means more than one filing and more than one fee, and the participant must be told so before paying.
Service on the State's Attorney at least 14 days before any hearing.
The hearing waiver requires the arrested person or defendant, the prosecutor AND any victim. All three must waive.
Prepare and file UJS-395 Notice of Entry after the order is signed, and mail it with the order to the State's Attorney.
scopeRestrictions: Expungement in South Dakota is sealing, not destruction, and the statute expressly says it does not imply physical destruction of records.

A nonpublic disposition record survives with the Division of Criminal Investigation for use by law enforcement, prosecutors and courts, including for sentencing on later offences, future SIS eligibility and habitual-offender determinations. This is the single most important disclosure in South Dakota.
South Dakota is not a broad adult conviction-expungement state and must never be described as one.

Pricing honesty. The UJS publishes the full packet, detailed instructions, a Guide and File document generator and a Self-Help Center with staff contact options, all free. LegalEase adds value through eligibility screening, the entire-dismissal analysis, arrest-record counting and expectation-setting, and should not charge as though it were producing documents the state already produces for nothing.

tracks.legalName: Expungement of Record on Completion of a Diversion Program (SDCL §§ 23A-3-35 to 23A-3-37)
tracks.publicName: Clear a record after completing a diversion program
tracks.mechanism: A person placed in a diversion program is eligible for expungement of the entire criminal record related to that arrest if they successfully completed all the terms of the program and have not been charged with any new crimes, except petty offences or minor traffic citations, within one year and thirty days from the date of successful completion. Where those requirements are met the State's Attorney shall file a dismissal of all charges related to the arrest and a notice of completion of the diversion program, and upon that filing the court shall grant the expungement without the filing of a motion or any further action by the court.
exclusions: Any new crime charged within one year and thirty days from successful completion, other than petty offences or minor traffic citations.
Incomplete diversion, or any term of the diversion programme not satisfied.
Anything short of the ENTIRE criminal record related to that arrest; the statute is framed around the entire record.

tracks.legalName: Automatic Removal of Non-Felony Charges or Convictions from the Public Record (SDCL § 23A-3-34)
tracks.publicName: Automatic removal of a minor case from your public record
tracks.mechanism: Any charge or conviction resulting from a case where a petty offense, municipal ordinance violation or a Class 2 misdemeanor was the highest charged offense shall be automatically removed from a defendant's public record after five years if all court-ordered conditions on the case have been satisfied and the defendant has not been convicted of any further offenses within those five years. The case record remains available to court personnel or as authorized by order of the court and may be used as an enhancement in the prosecution of subsequent offenses as provided by law.
exclusions: Any case where the highest charged offense exceeded a Class 2 misdemeanor.
Any case with court-ordered conditions that have not been satisfied.
Any defendant convicted of a further offense within the five-year period.
Removal from the public record does not remove the record from court personnel, from access by order of the court, or from use as an enhancement in a later prosecution.

tracks.legalName: Sealing of Records on Discharge and Dismissal after a Suspended Imposition of Sentence (SDCL §§ 23A-27-13 to 23A-27-17)
tracks.publicName: Seal a record after a suspended imposition of sentence
tracks.mechanism: For certain offenses a court may suspend imposition of sentence where the person has never before been convicted of a felony. After the person completes all court conditions the defendant is discharged and the case is dismissed without adjudication of guilt, and the discharge and dismissal are not deemed a conviction for disqualifications or disabilities imposed by law. Upon the discharge and dismissal a court SHALL order that all official records, other than the nonpublic records retained by the Division of Criminal Investigation, be sealed along with all records relating to the arrest, indictment or information, trial, finding of guilt, and dismissal and discharge. The order restores the person to the status occupied before arrest, indictment or information, and the person is not guilty of perjury or of giving a false statement for failing to recite or acknowledge the matter.
exclusions: Any person previously convicted of a felony, who is not eligible for a felony suspended imposition of sentence in the first place.
A second felony suspended imposition of sentence; the statute permits one felony SIS and one misdemeanor SIS per person.
Any case where the court conditions have not been completed and the discharge and dismissal have not issued.
The nonpublic records retained by the Division of Criminal Investigation, which are expressly excluded from the sealing order.
Federal, tribal, military and out-of-state records.

The section has now been read at the official South Dakota Legislature publication: 'Upon the discharge and dismissal of a person pursuant to § 23A-27-14, a court shall order that all official records ... be sealed'. Sealing is the court's obligation on discharge and dismissal; no participant motion exists. The unresolved fallback unit is therefore not carried, and the track is modelled as process_guidance. tracks.legalName: Sealing of Records on the Grant of a Chapter 24-14 Pardon (SDCL § 24-14-11)
tracks.publicName: Records sealed after a governor's pardon
tracks.mechanism: A person granted a pardon under the provisions of chapter 24-14 is released from all disabilities consequent on the conviction. Upon the granting of such a pardon the Governor shall order that all official records relating to the pardoned person's arrest, indictment or information, trial, finding of guilt, application for a pardon, and the proceedings of the Board of Pardons and Paroles be sealed. The Governor files a public document with the secretary of state certifying the pardon; that document remains public for five years and is then sealed. A pardon granted without following the provisions of the chapter may not be sealed. The pardon restores the person to their pre-arrest status and protects against perjury or false-statement liability for failing to acknowledge the matter, but the conviction may still be considered for sentencing on subsequent offences and habitual-offender determinations.
exclusions: Any pardon granted without following the provisions of chapter 24-14, which expressly may not be sealed.
The pardon application itself, which is a Board of Pardons and Paroles process requiring advocacy and is outside LegalEase self-help scope.
Federal, tribal, military and out-of-state records.

tracks.legalName: Immediate expunction order on acquittal in open court, T.C.A. § 40-32-106
tracks.publicName: The judge should clear your record the day you are found not guilty
tracks.mechanism: On a not-guilty verdict by judge or jury on all counts, the presiding judge must ask the acquitted person whether they want the records removed and destroyed, and if the answer is yes the court issues the order immediately with no separate petition. The section was renumbered by Public Chapter 268 of 2025, effective 2025-04-24: the acquittal ground that sat at former § 40-32-101(a) is now within § 40-32-106, whose non-conviction grounds include a verdict of not guilty, and which carries the acquittal-in-open-court procedure. No fee may be charged: § 40-32-106(a)(1) provides that qualifying public records must be removed and destroyed without cost to the person. Under § 40-32-110 expunction restores the person, in contemplation of law, to the status occupied before arrest, indictment, information, trial and conviction.
exclusions: A partial acquittal. The immediate route runs on a not-guilty verdict on all counts; a mixed-count case routes to the redaction analysis instead.
A person who was never asked at the verdict, or who declined at the time and later changed their mind. That person routes to the non-conviction petition track, which remains open.
This track offers no participant filing. The order issues in open court on the judge's own question.

waitingPeriods.duration: The not-guilty verdict itself. The order issues immediately in open court and there is no waiting period.

packetInstructions: Confirm the statutory citation with the county clerk or district attorney general before every filing. Chapter 32 was reorganized by Public Chapter 268 of 2025, effective 2025-04-24, and codified by Public Chapter 608, the 2026 Code Bill, effective 2026-03-25. Clerks and published guidance may still use the pre-reorganization numbering: the Tennessee AOC's own expunction page is titled to say updated information is coming to reflect changes to T.C.A. § 40-32-101 and still reasons from that section, which since 2025-04-24 has been nothing but a definitions section. A generated petition citing the wrong section is a rejection risk either way, so the packet is built to carry the current citation with the superseded one noted, and instructs the participant to confirm before filing.

Add T.C.A. § 40-6-204(b) to participant education: a person being charged with a crime must be informed that if the charges are dismissed or nolle prossed, or no charges are filed, they are entitled on request to removal and destruction of all public records without cost. Participants often do not know this was said to them. The current text of § 40-6-204 could not be retrieved from an official Tennessee source on 2026-08-06, so the packet names the right and its statutory home without quoting the provision.
scopeRestrictions: Expunction is not automatic. A dismissed charge or a completed diversion stays on background checks until a petition is filed. This is the most common Tennessee misunderstanding and the packet leads with it.
No reach to federal records; a diversion guilty plea may remain visible on clearance checks.

tracks.legalName: Free expunction of a non-conviction record by petition, T.C.A. § 40-32-106(a)
tracks.publicName: Clear a charge that did not end in a conviction
tracks.mechanism: Created by Public Chapter 268 of 2025, effective 2025-04-24, and codified by Public Chapter 608 effective 2026-03-25. All public records of a person charged with a misdemeanour or felony must, upon petition by that person to the court having jurisdiction in the previous action, be removed and destroyed without cost to the person where the charge was dismissed other than by diversion completion, a no true bill was returned, the person was arrested and released without being charged, a nolle prosequi was entered, a verdict of not guilty was returned, or on the section's further grounds including qualifying implied-consent dismissals, abatement by death, mistaken identity and racial-justice-protest convictions. Subsection (a)(2) extends the same no-cost treatment to a successfully defended order of protection and to expired bonds under § 38-3-109. There is no waiting period. The TBI certificate under § 40-32-102(c) is not required for a § 40-32-106 expunction unless the expunction resulted from successful completion of pretrial or judicial diversion. Under § 40-32-110 expunction restores the person, in contemplation of law, to the status occupied before arrest, indictment, information, trial and conviction, and under § 40-32-102(e) the expunged records are confidential and unlawful release is a Class A misdemeanour.
exclusions: A dismissal that resulted from successful completion of a diversion programme, which routes to the pretrial or judicial diversion tracks and carries a clerk's fee rather than being free.
Any count in the case that resulted in a conviction. A mixed-count case routes to the redaction analysis.
Records in a county other than the one where the case originated, which require a separate filing in each county.

An arrest for which the court with jurisdiction has no history within its records. Section 40-32-106 cannot reach it, because this petition runs to the court having jurisdiction in the previous action and there is no previous action in that court's records. That participant routes to tn_arrest_no_court_record under T.C.A. § 40-32-109, which is a different vehicle and is not free.

waitingPeriods.duration: None.
The court sends the order to the TBI within 30 days of entry. Nothing changes on a background check until it arrives.

tracks.venue: Statewide statute with originating-court venue. The petition goes to the court having jurisdiction in the previous action — the county criminal, circuit or general sessions court where the case originated. A person with cases in several counties files separately in each. There is no statewide participant form, so what varies locally is the clerk's own paperwork: the AOC directs filers to check with the court clerk because separate forms may be required for multiple charges.

destination.name: The county criminal, circuit or general sessions court having jurisdiction in the previous action
destination.detail: Confirmed on 2026-08-06 by direct inspection of both Tennessee AOC form indices: the self-help forms page publishes only divorce and order-of-protection forms, and the full forms-and-publications inventory covers appellate, divorce, general sessions civil, mediation, non-IV-D child support, order of protection, parenting plan and trial court forms, plus licensing forms. No expunction form appears in either. This is a negative finding established by inspection of the authoritative index, not by failure to search.

releaseBlockers.question: Current authority reveals statutory record-clearing routes that are outside the adopted nine-slot mechanism inventory and are therefore not built here. Public Chapter 268 created T.C.A. § 40-32-107(c), expunction after a conviction for illegal registration or voting under § 2-19-107 on a fifteen-year wait, and § 40-32-109, expunction of an arrest record where the court with jurisdiction has no record of the arrest, with a clerk search and certification. Public Chapter 719 rewrote the § 40-32-107(d) post-pardon route, replacing an open-textured judicial nonviolent-crime finding with a closed seven-item felony exclusion list, which substantially broadens it. Public Chapter 1061 added § 40-32-107(e), the recovery-court route, effective 2026-07-01 with no offence-date limitation. Each petitions under § 40-32-108. Adding any of them would change the adopted denominator, which a normalization worker may not do, so they are recorded for a captain-authorized inventory amendment instead.

releaseBlockers.question: Which participants presenting on the § 40-32-106(a)(1)(C) arrested-and-released-without-charge ground in fact have a court file and which do not. That ground reaches exactly the population most likely to have no court record, so the screening question is asked, but Tennessee publishes no way for a participant to confirm the answer before filing and no county practice was surveyed. The consequence is a routing risk between a free route and a fee-bearing one rather than a doubt about either mechanism.

provenance.sourceStatement: Add an exclusion and a routing cross-reference. Exclusion: an arrest for which the court with jurisdiction has no history within its records, which § 40-32-106 cannot reach because its petition runs to the court having jurisdiction in the previous action. Routing: send that participant to tn_arrest_no_court_record. Add a participant question asking whether any court file exists — whether the person was ever arraigned, ever appeared, ever received a case number — because the two routes differ in vehicle, in fee and in procedure, and § 40-32-106(a)(1)(C) reaches a person arrested and released without being charged, who is precisely the person most likely to have no court file. Add the fee disclosure: § 40-32-106 is free and § 40-32-109 is not.

legalDesignLimitations.statement: Narrowed by the integrated Tennessee 2026 route inventory decision. This route no longer reaches an arrest for which the court with jurisdiction has no history within its records; that population is governed by T.C.A. § 40-32-109 and routes to tn_arrest_no_court_record. The distinction is material to the participant in three ways: a different statutory vehicle, a mandatory clerk's fee where this route is free, and a clerk record-search and certification step that has no analogue here. The two mechanisms are not merged.

provenance.sourceStatement: Add an exclusion and a routing cross-reference. Exclusion: an arrest for which the court with jurisdiction has no history within its records, which § 40-32-106 cannot reach because its petition runs to the court having jurisdiction in the previous action. Routing: send that participant to tn_arrest_no_court_record. Add a participant question asking whether any court file exists — whether the person was ever arraigned, ever appeared, ever received a case number — because the two routes differ in vehicle, in fee and in procedure, and § 40-32-106(a)(1)(C) reaches a person arrested and released without being charged, who is precisely the person most likely to have no court file. Add the fee disclosure: § 40-32-106 is free and § 40-32-109 is not. Basis: T.C.A. § 40-32-109(a) read against § 40-32-106(a)(1).

Open question blocks release (correct_form): Whether any county requires a particular local form for a § 40-32-106 petition, and what it is. The AOC publishes no expunction form at all, confirmed on 2026-08-06, and directs filers to check with the court clerk because separate forms may be required for multiple charges. That makes local clerk paperwork the only form variable, and it is county-specific rather than statewide. No county form is adopted or promoted by this memo.

Open question blocks release (legal_effect_or_warning): Three ancillary current-text exports remain pending and are recorded as source-completeness follow-ups only, exactly as the captain-owned authority receipt directs. T.C.A. § 40-32-104 is the chapter's penalty provision, confirmed by the official cross-reference at new § 40-32-102(e)(2), which makes unlawful release of confidential expunged records a Class A misdemeanour punishable as described in § 40-32-104. T.C.A. § 40-6-204 could not be confirmed from any official Tennessee source and is not asserted; no official act retrieved cites, quotes or amends it. T.C.A. §§ 40-15-102 through 40-15-107 are the pretrial diversion scheme, confirmed by official cross-reference from the enacted text of Public Chapter 268 and by the TBI. None of the three is printed in the Code Bill extract and none is claimed to be. None is the vehicle for a participant-facing record-clearing route: the record-clearing consequence of completing pretrial diversion lives in Chapter 32 at § 40-32-106(d), not in Chapter 15. These do not reinstate the statewide codification blocker, which the captain receipt cleared.

Open question blocks release (governing_mechanism): Current authority reveals statutory record-clearing routes that are outside the adopted nine-slot mechanism inventory and are therefore not built here. Public Chapter 268 created T.C.A. § 40-32-107(c), expunction after a conviction for illegal registration or voting under § 2-19-107 on a fifteen-year wait, and § 40-32-109, expunction of an arrest record where the court with jurisdiction has no record of the arrest, with a clerk search and certification. Public Chapter 719 rewrote the § 40-32-107(d) post-pardon route, replacing an open-textured judicial nonviolent-crime finding with a closed seven-item felony exclusion list, which substantially broadens it. Public Chapter 1061 added § 40-32-107(e), the recovery-court route, effective 2026-07-01 with no offence-date limitation. Each petitions under § 40-32-108. Adding any of them would change the adopted denominator, which a normalization worker may not do, so they are recorded for a captain-authorized inventory amendment instead.

Open question blocks release (filing_process): Which participants presenting on the § 40-32-106(a)(1)(C) arrested-and-released-without-charge ground in fact have a court file and which do not. That ground reaches exactly the population most likely to have no court record, so the screening question is asked, but Tennessee publishes no way for a participant to confirm the answer before filing and no county practice was surveyed. The consequence is a routing risk between a free route and a fee-bearing one rather than a doubt about either mechanism.
One or more official sources have no recorded SHA-256, so staleness cannot be detected.

tracks.legalName: Expunction where the person was arrested or charged due to mistaken identity, T.C.A. § 40-32-106(a)(1)(H)
tracks.publicName: Clear an arrest that was not yours
tracks.mechanism: Mistaken identity is one of the enumerated non-conviction grounds in the reorganized § 40-32-106(a)(1), and Public Chapter 268 of 2025 rewrote § 40-32-101 as a chapter-wide definitions section that defines mistaken identity for the whole chapter. Relief runs on the same free petition vehicle as the other non-conviction grounds, with an added factual showing that the person was arrested or charged because of a case of mistaken identity. The pre-reorganization provision the controlling review cited, former § 40-32-101(a)(1)(C)(i), also allowed the petitioner to provide evidence of the circumstances and request that the court order the expunction be expedited, on which finding the court was to order the TBI and any other expunging entity to act in an expedited manner. Whether that expedited-order duty survived the reorganization in the same terms was not established from an official source on 2026-08-06, and it is not asserted here.
exclusions: Any case where the participant was in fact the person arrested or charged.
Any case where the participant's information is on the record for a reason other than mistaken identity, which routes to the ordinary non-conviction grounds.
Any dispute about identity, which is a factual contest rather than a showing.

packetInstructions: Confirm the statutory citation with the county clerk or district attorney general before every filing. Chapter 32 was reorganized by Public Chapter 268 of 2025, effective 2025-04-24, and codified by Public Chapter 608, the 2026 Code Bill, effective 2026-03-25. Clerks and published guidance may still use the pre-reorganization numbering: the Tennessee AOC's own expunction page is titled to say updated information is coming to reflect changes to T.C.A. § 40-32-101 and still reasons from that section, which since 2025-04-24 has been nothing but a definitions section. A generated petition citing the wrong section is a rejection risk either way, so the packet is built to carry the current citation with the superseded one noted, and instructs the participant to confirm before filing.

tracks.publicName: Clear the dismissed counts in a case where other counts stuck
tracks.mechanism: The controlling review identified this remedy from a secondary profile and left its citation unresolved as the highest-value Tennessee research item. It is resolved: Public Chapter 268 of 2025 created a partial database removal provision at T.C.A. § 40-32-106(c)(2), and the TBI's own form BI-0334, revision 04/2025, is captioned Removal of Criminal Offender Record pursuant to T.C.A. § 40-32-106(c)(2), which corroborates both the citation and the mechanism from an official source. The remedy answers the most common real-world Tennessee scenario after a clean dismissal: a multi-count case where some counts were dismissed as part of a plea and others produced a conviction. Whether the relief reaches paper records or only electronic databases was not established, and the review flags that limitation as materially changing what a participant gets.
exclusions: A case in which no count resulted in a conviction, which routes to the ordinary free non-conviction petition and gets the fuller remedy.
The counts that produced the conviction. Those are untouched by this route and are eligible only through the conviction-expunction analysis, if at all.
Any expectation of full expunction. This is partial removal of the non-conviction counts, and on the current record it reaches electronic databases with paper coverage unconfirmed.

tracks.legalName: Expunction of an arrest record where the court has no history of the arrest, T.C.A. § 40-32-109
tracks.publicName: Clear an arrest that never reached a courtroom
tracks.mechanism: Expunction of the arrest record, with the § 40-32-110 effect expressly applied by § 40-32-109(f): the petitioner is entitled to have all public records destroyed, is restored in contemplation of law to the status occupied before the arrest, must not suffer adverse effects or collateral disabilities by virtue of the offence, and is not guilty of perjury for failing to acknowledge the arrest in response to any inquiry. A person whose arrest record exists but for whom the court with jurisdiction over the offence for which the person was arrested has no history of the arrest within the court's records. This is the participant whose arrest never produced a court file — the case that the § 40-32-106 route cannot reach, because that route runs to the court having jurisdiction in the previous action and here there is no previous action in that court's records. This is the only one of the four additions that does NOT run through § 40-32-108, and it is the only Tennessee route in the entire chapter on which the participant writes the operative petition. Section 40-32-109 contains no cross-reference to § 40-32-108 of any kind, so § 40-32-108(e) — under which the office of the district attorney general must prepare the petition and proposed order — does not reach it. It also carries no waiting period, no 61-day pre-order clock, no rebuttable presumption and no two-year refiling bar, all of which live in § 40-32-108 alone. Section 40-32-109(a) uses the permissive 'may petition', where § 40-32-108(a) uses 'shall petition'. Codified through Public Chapter 608. Untouched by Public Chapters 719, 930 and 1061. Six subsections, (a) through (f), with no further subdivision numbering.
exclusions: Any arrest for which the court with jurisdiction does have a history within its records. That participant is on the § 40-32-106 analysis, and on the free route rather than this fee-bearing one.

Any case that reached the court and was dismissed, no-true-billed, nolle prossed or resolved by acquittal or by release without charge that the court did record. Those grounds are § 40-32-106(a)(1) and are free.
Any case that came through a diversion programme, which is § 40-32-106(d) and carries its own clerk's fee and TBI certificate requirement.

Any expectation that the district attorney general will prepare the petition. Section 40-32-109 contains no cross-reference to § 40-32-108, so the § 40-32-108(e) preparation duty does not reach this route and the participant prepares the petition.

tracks.venue: The court with jurisdiction over the offence for which the person was arrested, per § 40-32-109(a). The section states that forum inside the eligibility clause rather than as a standalone filing directive, and supplies it by implication: it is the court whose records the clerk searches under (c) and whose clerk serves the district attorney general under (a). Service is on the district attorney general for that judicial district, which is the only express geographic anchor. There is no residence-based venue and no alternative forum.

destination.name: The court with jurisdiction over the offence for which the person was arrested, filed through its clerk
destination.detail: Upon filing, the clerk serves the petition on the district attorney general for that judicial district. Both the petitioner and the district attorney general may file evidence. The clerk's office searches the court's records and certifies to the court whether there is any history of the arrest. The court reviews the clerk's certification and all evidence, and may enter the order if it finds there is no history of the arrest within the court's record. The petition on this route is the participant's own operative statutory petition, not a request to another office: § 40-32-109 contains no cross-reference to § 40-32-108, so the district-attorney preparation duty at § 40-32-108(e) does not govern here. The clerk's certification under (c) and the court's order under (d) remain instruments of their own actors and neither is generated or pre-completed.

In which county did the arrest happen, and which court would have had jurisdiction over that offence?
Were you ever arraigned, did you ever appear in court, and were you ever given a court date or a case number for this arrest?
As far as you know, does any court file or court case exist for this arrest?
What is the state control number on your TBI criminal history, and what does that history show about this arrest?

Did this arrest end in a dismissal, a no true bill, a nolle prosequi, an acquittal, or a release without charge that the court actually recorded? If it did, the free § 40-32-106 route is the right one instead.
Is there anything you can file that bears on there being no court record — a letter from a clerk, a records search result, anything else?
generationRequirements.conditionDescription: Asked because § 40-32-109(b) permits the petitioner to file evidence, not because anything is required.

participantFilingRequirements.name: TBI criminal history
participantFilingRequirements.obtainedFrom: Tennessee Bureau of Investigation
participantFilingRequirements.howToObtain: Order the TBI criminal history first. It is what shows the arrest record exists at all, and it supplies the state control number referenced in T.C.A. § 8-4-115. Without it the participant cannot show there is an arrest record to expunge. LegalEase never receives, inspects or authenticates it.

participantFilingRequirements.obtainedFrom: The agency that made the arrest
participantFilingRequirements.howToObtain: Ask the arresting agency for what it holds. LegalEase names the kinds of material that bear on the point and does nothing more: it never assembles, reviews or vouches for any of it.

participantFilingRequirements.obtainedFrom: The participant's own records, or a clerk asked informally whether a file exists

participantFilingRequirements.howToObtain: The participant gathers whatever they have. LegalEase does not judge whether it is sufficient and does not assert what the clerk's search will find.

manualCompletionItems.item: The account of the arrest and of what the participant knows about the absence of any court record

manualCompletionItems.item: The state control number referenced in T.C.A. § 8-4-115

selfHelpBoundaries: The court does in fact have a record of the arrest. That takes the participant out of this route entirely and into the § 40-32-106 analysis, which is the free route; the participant is redirected there rather than handed off.

The district attorney general files evidence that the court does have a history of the arrest. That converts the matter into a contested question of fact and the participant is handed off to an attorney.

Whether a prior court action or court file ever existed is disputed. LegalEase does not adjudicate that question: the clerk searches and certifies and the court finds, so a disputed history is handed off to an attorney.

packetInstructions: No TBI certificate step arises on this route. Section 40-32-102(c)(1) expressly exempts the court from submitting a certificate where the expungement is pursuant to § 40-32-109, and § 40-32-109(d) directs the court to review only the clerk's certification and the evidence submitted.

Payment of the clerk's fee under T.C.A. § 8-21-401, which § 40-32-109(e) makes mandatory. There is no indigency, waiver or without-cost provision in § 40-32-109, in express contrast to § 40-32-106(a)(1). The participant must be told this route is not free before anything is prepared.
scopeRestrictions: This is the only one of the four additions that does NOT run through § 40-32-108, and it is the only Tennessee route in the entire chapter on which the participant writes the operative petition. Section 40-32-109 contains no cross-reference to § 40-32-108 of any kind, so § 40-32-108(e) — under which the office of the district attorney general must prepare the petition and proposed order — does not reach it. It also carries no waiting period, no 61-day pre-order clock, no rebuttable presumption and no two-year refiling bar, all of which live in § 40-32-108 alone. Section 40-32-109(a) uses the permissive 'may petition', where § 40-32-108(a) uses 'shall petition'.

LegalEase does not create a clerk certification, does not make judicial findings, does not certify eligibility and promises neither filing nor relief. Whether a prior court action or court file ever existed is not something LegalEase adjudicates: the clerk searches and certifies, and the court finds.

provenance.sourceStatement: This addendum specifies routes. It does not build them. No packet was implemented, no route was promoted, no source was promoted, no migration was run and nothing was deployed. No participant filing is invented anywhere in it. On Routes 1, 2 and 3 the operative petition and proposed order are prepared by the office of the district attorney general under § 40-32-108(e), and the generated artifact is the participant's request and eligibility record. On Route 4 the participant does write the petition, because § 40-32-109 contains no cross-reference to § 40-32-108 and no provision assigning preparation to anyone else — but the clerk's record search and certification under (c) and the court's order under (d) remain instruments of their own actors and neither is generated. The TBI certificate, the TBI expungement order, the district attorney's petition and the clerk's certification are each identified as instruments of their own actor and none is generated.

tracks.legalName: Expunction after successful completion of pretrial diversion, T.C.A. § 40-32-106(d)
tracks.publicName: Clear a case after completing pretrial diversion
tracks.mechanism: Prosecution is suspended under a memorandum of understanding with the district attorney general; the person does not plead guilty and is not found guilty. On successful completion the charges are dismissed, and under T.C.A. § 40-32-106(d)(1) the person may then petition for expunction of the public records where the charges were dismissed as a result of successful completion of a pretrial diversion programme pursuant to §§ 40-15-102 through 40-15-107. The provision is permissive as to filing and mandatory as to nothing: a petition is required and expunction is not automatic. Section 40-32-106(d)(3) requires the appropriate clerk's fee under § 8-21-401, so unlike a straight dismissal this route is not free. Section 40-32-106(d)(2) bars expunction where the diverted offence was a sexual offence or a violent sexual offence as defined in § 40-39-202. The TBI certificate under § 40-32-102(c) is required here, because the exemption for § 40-32-106 expunctions is expressly carved back where the expunction resulted from successful completion of pretrial diversion.
exclusions: A diversion that was not successfully completed. Where the diversionary period is not completed the sentence goes into effect and the offence is not expunged.

An offence that was a sexual offence or a violent sexual offence as defined in T.C.A. § 40-39-202. Section 40-32-106(d)(2) bars expunction of a diverted case on that ground even though the offence could be diverted, which is the trap that catches people who completed diversion and are still stuck.
A dismissal that did not follow diversion, which routes to the free non-conviction petition instead and carries no clerk's fee.

waitingPeriods.duration: Successful completion of the diversion programme and dismissal of the charges. There is no further waiting period, but a petition is still required and nothing happens without one.

Required on this route. The § 40-32-102(c) exemption for § 40-32-106 expunctions does not apply where the expunction resulted from successful completion of diversion, so the court must obtain and attach the certificate before entering the order.
The court sends the order to the TBI within 30 days of entry.

tracks.venue: Statewide statute with originating-court venue. The petition goes to the court having jurisdiction in the previous action — the county criminal, circuit or general sessions court where the case originated. A person with cases in several counties files separately in each. There is no statewide participant form, so what varies locally is the clerk's own paperwork: the AOC directs filers to check with the court clerk because separate forms may be required for multiple charges.

destination.name: The county criminal, circuit or general sessions court having jurisdiction in the previous action
destination.detail: Confirmed on 2026-08-06 by direct inspection of both Tennessee AOC form indices: the self-help forms page publishes only divorce and order-of-protection forms, and the full forms-and-publications inventory covers appellate, divorce, general sessions civil, mediation, non-IV-D child support, order of protection, parenting plan and trial court forms, plus licensing forms. No expunction form appears in either. This is a negative finding established by inspection of the authoritative index, not by failure to search.

packetInstructions: Confirm the statutory citation with the county clerk or district attorney general before every filing. Chapter 32 was reorganized by Public Chapter 268 of 2025, effective 2025-04-24, and codified by Public Chapter 608, the 2026 Code Bill, effective 2026-03-25. Clerks and published guidance may still use the pre-reorganization numbering: the Tennessee AOC's own expunction page is titled to say updated information is coming to reflect changes to T.C.A. § 40-32-101 and still reasons from that section, which since 2025-04-24 has been nothing but a definitions section. A generated petition citing the wrong section is a rejection risk either way, so the packet is built to carry the current citation with the superseded one noted, and instructs the participant to confirm before filing.

A petition is still required after diversion. Completing diversion dismisses the case but leaves it visible until a separate expunction petition is filed, and this is the second most common Tennessee misunderstanding after the not-automatic point.

The order of expungement is marked Suspension of Prosecution § 40-15-105 for a pretrial diversion case, which is how the TBI records it. The marking requirement is part of the court's instrument rather than the participant's.
scopeRestrictions: Expunction is not automatic. A dismissed charge or a completed diversion stays on background checks until a petition is filed. This is the most common Tennessee misunderstanding and the packet leads with it.
No reach to federal records; a diversion guilty plea may remain visible on clearance checks.

Sexual offences as defined by the sex offender registry statute can be diverted but cannot be expunged. Section 40-32-106(d)(2) bars expunction of a diverted case on that ground, so a person can complete diversion on such an offence and still be unable to clear the record. This must be in the diversion copy.

releaseBlockers.question: Three ancillary current-text exports remain pending and are recorded as source-completeness follow-ups only, exactly as the captain-owned authority receipt directs. T.C.A. § 40-32-104 is the chapter's penalty provision, confirmed by the official cross-reference at new § 40-32-102(e)(2), which makes unlawful release of confidential expunged records a Class A misdemeanour punishable as described in § 40-32-104. T.C.A. § 40-6-204 could not be confirmed from any official Tennessee source and is not asserted; no official act retrieved cites, quotes or amends it. T.C.A. §§ 40-15-102 through 40-15-107 are the pretrial diversion scheme, confirmed by official cross-reference from the enacted text of Public Chapter 268 and by the TBI. None of the three is printed in the Code Bill extract and none is claimed to be. None is the vehicle for a participant-facing record-clearing route: the record-clearing consequence of completing pretrial diversion lives in Chapter 32 at § 40-32-106(d), not in Chapter 15. These do not reinstate the statewide codification blocker, which the captain receipt cleared.

tracks.legalName: Expunction after successful completion of judicial diversion, T.C.A. § 40-32-106(d) and § 40-35-313
tracks.publicName: Clear a case after completing judicial diversion
tracks.mechanism: Judicial diversion under T.C.A. § 40-35-313 is a conditional guilty plea with no judgment of conviction entered: the court defers adjudication and places the person on probation, typically six to eighteen months, and on successful completion discharges and dismisses the case. A completed judicial diversion is not a conviction under Tennessee law. Under § 40-32-106(d)(1) the person may then petition for expunction where the charges were dismissed as a result of successful completion of a judicial diversion programme pursuant to § 40-35-313. Public Chapter 268 amended § 40-35-313(b) and (c) to replace the old § 40-32-101 subdivision citations with references to § 40-32-101 and to title 40, chapter 32, which is the official cross-reference confirming the route survived the reorganization. The clerk's fee under § 8-21-401 applies, the TBI certificate is required, and the § 40-32-106(d)(2) sexual-offence bar applies here too. Federal systems and security-clearance background checks may still see the underlying guilty plea, which should be stated to every judicial diversion participant.
exclusions: A diversion that was not successfully completed. Where the diversionary period is not completed the sentence goes into effect and the offence is not expunged.

An offence that was a sexual offence or a violent sexual offence as defined in T.C.A. § 40-39-202. Section 40-32-106(d)(2) bars expunction of a diverted case on that ground even though the offence could be diverted, which is the trap that catches people who completed diversion and are still stuck.
A dismissal that did not follow diversion, which routes to the free non-conviction petition instead and carries no clerk's fee.
A person whose probationary period was not successfully completed, in which case the sentence goes into effect and the offence is not expunged.

Offences for which judicial diversion itself is unavailable, including Class A or B felonies, sexual offences, DUI, vehicular assault, child abuse, a prior felony conviction, a prior Class A misdemeanour conviction that included jail time, or any prior diversion.

waitingPeriods.duration: Successful completion of the diversion programme and dismissal of the charges. There is no further waiting period, but a petition is still required and nothing happens without one.

Required on this route. The § 40-32-102(c) exemption for § 40-32-106 expunctions does not apply where the expunction resulted from successful completion of diversion, so the court must obtain and attach the certificate before entering the order.
The court sends the order to the TBI within 30 days of entry.

tracks.venue: Statewide statute with originating-court venue. The petition goes to the court having jurisdiction in the previous action — the county criminal, circuit or general sessions court where the case originated. A person with cases in several counties files separately in each. There is no statewide participant form, so what varies locally is the clerk's own paperwork: the AOC directs filers to check with the court clerk because separate forms may be required for multiple charges.

destination.name: The county criminal, circuit or general sessions court having jurisdiction in the previous action
destination.detail: Confirmed on 2026-08-06 by direct inspection of both Tennessee AOC form indices: the self-help forms page publishes only divorce and order-of-protection forms, and the full forms-and-publications inventory covers appellate, divorce, general sessions civil, mediation, non-IV-D child support, order of protection, parenting plan and trial court forms, plus licensing forms. No expunction form appears in either. This is a negative finding established by inspection of the authoritative index, not by failure to search.

packetInstructions: Confirm the statutory citation with the county clerk or district attorney general before every filing. Chapter 32 was reorganized by Public Chapter 268 of 2025, effective 2025-04-24, and codified by Public Chapter 608, the 2026 Code Bill, effective 2026-03-25. Clerks and published guidance may still use the pre-reorganization numbering: the Tennessee AOC's own expunction page is titled to say updated information is coming to reflect changes to T.C.A. § 40-32-101 and still reasons from that section, which since 2025-04-24 has been nothing but a definitions section. A generated petition citing the wrong section is a rejection risk either way, so the packet is built to carry the current citation with the superseded one noted, and instructs the participant to confirm before filing.

A petition is still required after diversion. Completing diversion dismisses the case but leaves it visible until a separate expunction petition is filed, and this is the second most common Tennessee misunderstanding after the not-automatic point.
Federal systems and security-clearance background checks may still see the underlying guilty plea from a judicial diversion. That should be stated to every judicial diversion participant.
scopeRestrictions: Expunction is not automatic. A dismissed charge or a completed diversion stays on background checks until a petition is filed. This is the most common Tennessee misunderstanding and the packet leads with it.
No reach to federal records; a diversion guilty plea may remain visible on clearance checks.

Sexual offences as defined by the sex offender registry statute can be diverted but cannot be expunged. Section 40-32-106(d)(2) bars expunction of a diverted case on that ground, so a person can complete diversion on such an offence and still be unable to clear the record. This must be in the diversion copy.

tracks.legalName: Expunction of an eligible conviction, T.C.A. § 40-32-107(a) with procedure at § 40-32-108
tracks.publicName: Expunge an eligible conviction
tracks.mechanism: Public Chapter 268 of 2025 split the former § 40-32-101(g) conviction route along an eligibility and procedure seam: § 40-32-107 now defines who is an eligible petitioner and § 40-32-108 supplies the whole procedure. That mapping is officially corroborated rather than inferred — Public Chapter 268's own conforming amendments replaced the old citation to § 40-32-101(g)(3) with § 40-32-107 and the old § 40-32-101(g) with § 40-32-107(a)(1), and replaced procedural references to § 40-32-101 with § 40-32-108. Eligibility under § 40-32-107(a) turns on the offence being on one of the enumerated Class C, Class D or Class E felony lists or within the misdemeanour category subject to its exclusion list, the offence having occurred on or after 1 November 1989 and prior to any conviction for an expunction-ineligible offence including federal and out-of-state offences, no previous expunction under subsection (a), (b) or (c), and fulfilment of every sentence requirement including all fines, restitution, court costs and other assessments, completion of imprisonment or probation, all release conditions, and any required year free from dependency on or abuse of alcohol or a controlled substance. The waiting period at § 40-32-107(a)(3)(B) runs from completion of the sentence: five years for a misdemeanour or Class E felony and ten years for a Class C or Class D felony. Subsection (a)(4) directs the petitioner to § 40-32-108, whose subsection (e) requires the petition and proposed order to be prepared by the office of the district attorney general and given to the petitioner to file. Public Chapter 719, effective 2026-04-14, rewrote the § 40-32-108(d)(2) decision standard, preserving the rebuttable presumption for petitioners eligible under § 40-32-107(a)(1)(A) to (E) while directing the court to weigh the petitioner's interest against the best interests of justice and public safety. Public Chapter 930, effective 2026-07-01 and applying only to offences committed on or after that date, relocated burglary under § 39-13-1002 from the Class E list to the Class D list, which doubles the wait for that offence from five to ten years prospectively only.
exclusions: Any conviction that is not on the enumerated eligible lists at T.C.A. § 40-32-107(a)(1), which are section-specific Class C, Class D and Class E felony lists and a misdemeanour category subject to a long exclusion list.
DUI under T.C.A. § 55-10-401 and related serious traffic offences, which appear in the misdemeanour exclusion list.
Sexual offences and any offence requiring sex offender registration.
Class A and Class B felonies, violent offences and crimes against the person enumerated in the statute.
Vehicular assault and vehicular homicide.
Domestic assault under T.C.A. § 39-13-111, stalking under § 39-17-315, protective-order violations, and certain offences against children, all of which appear in the misdemeanour exclusion list.
Offences committed by a public official in an official capacity.
A conviction that did not occur on or after 1 November 1989, unless it satisfies the separate pre-1989 route at § 40-32-107(a)(1)(E) and its nine substantive tests.
A person who has previously been granted expunction under § 40-32-107(a), (b) or (c). The bars are reciprocal and lifetime.

A person holding a commercial driver licence convicted of a controlled-substance offence occurring in a motor vehicle, or holding any licence where the offence occurred in a commercial motor vehicle, under § 40-32-107(a)(2).

waitingPeriods.duration: Five years from completion of the sentence, measured at the time of filing.

waitingPeriods.duration: Ten years from completion of the sentence, measured at the time of filing.

waitingPeriods.duration: Ten years. Public Chapter 930 moved the offence from the Class E list to the Class D list for offences committed on or after 2026-07-01 only. An offence committed before that date is unaffected and the change is not applied retroactively.
On completion of the entire sentence, including all fines, restitution, court costs and other assessments. Outstanding amounts mean the sentence is not complete and the clock has not started.
The court may not order sooner than 61 days after the petition is served on the district attorney general, who has 60 days to submit recommendations.
No further petition for at least two years from the date of the denial, under § 40-32-108(d)(3).

tracks.venue: Statewide statute with originating-court venue and prosecutor-office routing. The request goes to the office of the district attorney general for the judicial district of the convicting court, because § 40-32-108(e) makes that office the preparer of the petition. The petition, once prepared, is filed by the petitioner with the clerk of the convicting court under § 40-32-108(a). A person with convictions in several judicial districts deals with each separately.

destination.name: The office of the district attorney general for the judicial district of the convicting court
destination.detail: Section 40-32-108(e) requires the petition and proposed order to be prepared by the district attorney general's office and given to the petitioner to be filed with the clerk. Both the Tennessee AOC and the TBI direct participants to request a conviction expungement packet from that office. LegalEase generates the participant's request and eligibility record; it does not generate the petition or the order, because those are prosecutor and court instruments.

generationRequirements.question: Which court handled the case, and in which county? A separate filing is needed in each county where you have a case.
What is the docket or case number?
What was the charge, and exactly how did the case end?
On what date did the case end?
What is the state control number on your TBI criminal history? The expunction order cannot be completed without it.
List every other conviction you have anywhere, including federal and out-of-state.
Are you asking about this because of immigration, federal employment or a security clearance? Tennessee expunction does not reach federal records.
What is the exact T.C.A. section you were convicted under? The offence name and class are not enough — Tennessee's eligible lists are section by section.
On what date was the offence committed? This matters independently of the conviction date, because a 2026 change applies only to offences committed on or after 1 July 2026.
Did the conviction occur on or after 1 November 1989?
On what date did you finish the entire sentence — including any imprisonment or probation, all release conditions, and every fine, restitution amount, court cost and other assessment?
Is every fine, restitution amount, court cost and other assessment paid in full? Anything outstanding means the sentence is not complete and the clock has not started.

Have you ever had a conviction expunged in Tennessee before under T.C.A. § 40-32-107(a), (b), (c) or (e)? This route is available once in a lifetime and a previous grant under (a), (b) or (c) closes it. A grant under (e) is recorded because the statute is asymmetric on the point, and no bar is applied against you that the subsection does not state.
Did you hold a commercial driver licence at the time, and did the offence involve a controlled substance or a commercial motor vehicle?
Did your sentence require a period free from dependency on or abuse of alcohol or a controlled substance? If so, have you met at least one year of it?
Was the conviction for burglary under T.C.A. § 39-13-1002? If so, the date of the offence decides whether the wait is five years or ten.
Have you received a pardon from the Governor for this conviction? If you have, a different route may reach it even where this one cannot.

If a DUI conviction is what is standing in the way: have you successfully completed a certified recovery court programme, and did the offence you want cleared happen at least ten years after that DUI conviction?

Mapping the offence to its exact T.C.A. section and checking it against the current eligible list is not something an offence label or class can settle. The eligible lists at T.C.A. § 40-32-107(a)(1) are enumerated section by section — Class C, Class D and Class E felony lists and a misdemeanour category with a long exclusion list — and the legislature has expanded them repeatedly, most recently by Public Chapter 930. The packet checks the current list rather than assuming, and any borderline offence goes to review.

Under T.C.A. § 40-32-108(e) the petition and proposed order must be prepared by the office of the district attorney general and given to the petitioner to be filed with the clerk of the court. The petition is therefore a prosecutor instrument, and LegalEase does not generate it. What LegalEase generates is the participant's own written request to the district attorney general's office for the conviction-expunction packet, with the supporting eligibility record. Both the Tennessee AOC and the TBI direct participants to request a conviction expungement packet from the district attorney's office, which is the practical face of that provision.
